The Necessary Ingredients for Success of Women in
Computing: A 360° Perspective from Students, Professionals
and Stakeholders
NOVA AHMED, DIAL, ECE, North South University, Dhaka, Bangladesh
TASMIAH TAHSIN MAYEESHA, ICT Ministry, Dhaka, Bangladesh
IFTI AZAD ABEER, DIAL, ECE, North South University, Dhaka, Bangladesh
ANIK SINHA, DIAL, ECE, North South University, Dhaka, Bangladesh
ANIK SAHA, DIAL, ECE, North South University, Dhaka, Bangladesh
The underrepresentation of women in computing in the workplace requires an understanding of the adequate
elements needed for women to succeed in Bangladesh complementing the existing body of work. It uses a var-
ied modality of communication Fictional inquiry (FI), where participants write letters to fictional characters
followed by a Co-design of solutions. This research considers N=71 participants, 48 tertiary-level computer
science and engineering students, and 23 stakeholders covering academics, computing professionals, and
guardians of women in computing over a period of one and a half years. The study identifies three major
elements for women in computing to succeed professionally: provision to improve skills and self-efficacy, en-
suring ways to increase the sense of belonging, and providing transportation and safety aligning through the
women’s empowerment framework of Naila Kabeer. The required elements for success and empowerment
show that a collaborative approach of support is required from families, institutes, and authorities from a
regional perspective that can be of interest to researchers from the HCI, CSCW, and ICTD fields. This work
is further expected to provide a guideline for stakeholders, policymakers, institutions, and families eager to
ensure inclusive learning and growing space for women in computing.
CCS Concepts: • Human-centered computing → Empirical studies in HCI;
Additional Key Words and Phrases: Women in computing, empowerment, Bangladesh, collaborative support,
inclusive learning

1 Introduction
Extensive research has focused on women in computing, particularly on existing challenges
[52, 56]. The challenges women in computing face comprise of social challenges interlinked with
numerous structural barriers that impact women and marginal communities disproportionately
[56, 100, 116]. Sometimes, the negative stereotype around women comes in subtle forms through
humor that makes it harder to address [31]. The barriers exist for women worldwide, including
resourceful regions, where a special emphasis focuses on female high school students as seen in
New Zealand or USA [49, 107]. In a developed region, the challenge can be wider for societally
marginal ones. On the other hand, in resource limited regions, there are challenges with access-
ing adequate resources as can be seen in South Africa [60] or in Sub-Saharan Africa [83] among
many other barriers. It shows that the challenges and practices for women in computing are deeply
rooted. Moreover, the impact of the barriers varies across regions, considering their support sys-
tems to accommodate them. The social values, customs, and incentives to have a safe career -in
terms of societal acceptance, harassment-free and limited mobility - all play a vital role for women
to take on a career in computing [56]. A close look at the barriers shows that the solutions require
collaborative support to ensure pathways to success for women in computing. In this work, we
take a look at women in computing living in Bangladesh, a South Asian Muslim major country,
where the social regulations impact women heavily [108, 109, 120]; focusing more on ingredients
of success while taking into account the existing barriers.
In this work’s social and regional context, the South Asian value system and Muslim women’s
regulations are considered. Existing work based on South Asian region, shows how women are
restricted from technology usage by social barriers and vulnerable to technology based abuse and
harassment [108, 109]. Technology-based abuse and harassment have impacted women to freely
express their feelings on open technology platforms or has restricted them from sharing their iden-
tities as women as has been seen in Bangladesh and other low-resource regions [42, 86]. It not only
creates barrier for women to access technology, it also hampers women’s possible future access to
technology. As a result, it creates technology dependencies on the male members of households,
showing a tendency towards supportive masculinity where male members or dominant members
take charge in the form of support [38, 108]. It takes a prominent form if religious justifications are
considered. For example, in Pakistan, Muslim women depend on technology access and operations
on male family members as it also aligns with religious values [67].
However, the picture is different when women in computing is considered, in many cases the en-
gagement is more active with a vision towards a better future. In India, where social barriers restrict
women from accessing technology in general [108, 109], there is a greater incentive for women to
have a secure earning in a career in computing that increases social values [131]. Similarly, women
in Afghanistan, prior to the Taliban regime, have shown to actively engage in the technology space,
in the hope to support other women alongside [9]. The positive engagement of women in comput-
ing is present in few other Muslim countries as well. Muslim countries like Iran, and Malaysia show
a large number of women in computing, with the presence of religious values applicable specifi-
cally towards women (e.g., as seen in [85]), where the motivation lies in being able to have a secure
desk job that meets the religious and social requirements [56]. On the other hand, Nepal, a coun-
try in South Asia, shows economic barriers and social rules that hamper the pathways to careers
for women in computing [115]. The picture is similar in Bangladesh as we explore the situation
for women in computing. We refer to women in computing as women pursuing education and ca-
reers in Computer Science, Computer Engineering, Computer Science and Engineering, IT, ICT, or
closely related fields in general our research study focuses on women with a background of Com-
puter Science and Engineering (CSE) discipline, a popular subject in the context of Bangladesh.

We want to take a close look at Bangladesh, a country sharing many South Asian social-cultural
norms for women in technology usage [108, 109] and being a Muslim major country with patriar-
chal practices [120, 122], trying to understand the key factors required for women in computing to
succeed. Scholarly exploration on Bangladeshi women in computing shows the existence of social
barriers such as the acceptable role of women, the necessity to ensure work-career balance; struc-
tural barriers like lack of safety, and the presence of sexual harassment for women [5, 6, 8, 68, 105,
121, 128]. These barriers impact women’s access to resources significantly. For example, there are
social perceptions that limits female students ability by making them to believe that they are “less
competent” compared to their male peers [68] or consideration of professional women to be “less
intelligent” [5]. Moreover, the structural barriers show resource challenges such as lack of access
to computing labs and lack of support for women in tech-professions [5, 8, 128]. There have been
initiatives to actively engage women in computing through dedicated activities such as female-
only classrooms [68], female-only programming contests [128], structured training activities for
women [8] in Bangladesh. The existing body of work looked at the existing barriers and proposed
various solutions to them. This work, on the other hand, engages the participants in designing the
solutions along with looking at the problems. This work complements the existing set of work by
exploring the elements needed to succeed as a woman in computing living in Bangladesh.
Given all the existing barriers, what are the necessary elements that would ensure success
for a woman in computing is the question this research aims to address. Success, in this work,
refers to the minimum expectation of ensuring a woman in computing enters her professional
life. Since the entire work considers women in computing, we discuss students, professionals, and
stakeholders (e.g., Graduate students, Software engineers, Parents, University faculties) related to
women in computing without referring to it repeatedly. This work takes a 360-degree perspective
taking into account the viewpoints of tertiary level students all across the country; all studying in
the field of computing along with professionals considering faculties, industry professionals, and
graduate students; and finally, the stakeholders, including views of parents and administrators.
In many cases, participants hold multiple roles and viewpoints, such as being an academic
and administrator or being a graduate student and holding an academic position, for example.
Considering the existing body of knowledge focusing on challenges and ways to mitigate them for
Bangladeshi women in computing [5, 6, 8, 68, 105, 121, 128], we wanted to use a varied approach
to understand the current status. We have considered a methodological variation in our work
using Fictional Inquiry (FI) that considers an imaginary prompt to explore a difficult topic [47].
It is inspired by a prior work conducted in the same regional context that explores difficult topics
using some storytelling indirections, which easily opens up many personalized feelings (as seen in
different works [4, 10, 11]). The FI were used in the research to understand the subtle barriers and
challenges that women face in the context of Bangladesh. We wanted the participants to bypass
existing socio-cultural norms or structures by prompting them with partially fictional artifacts
or scenarios used in FI. By doing fictional inquiry, we found strong emotional responses towards
authoritative figures such as teachers and parents, and infrastructural issues of educational insti-
tutions. Once we knew the barriers from FI, this work aimed to complement the existing literature
by co-designing solutions related to the barriers with female students in computing to include
their voices. It also engages the tertiary students in computing in co-design processes that would
enable them to reach their goals [135]. We use the findings from FI and the co-design process to
guide us through the current scenarios and develop discussion points to engage with professionals
and stakeholders, working as a team to find out the elements required for success that complement
existing exploration.
This work considers N=71 participants, 48 tertiary-level female computer science and engineer-
ing students, and 23 stakeholders consisting of parents, faculties, administrators, and professionals.

The student participants are from four major regions - Dhaka, Chottogram, Sylhet, and Rajshahi
across Bangladesh. These participants engage in fictional inquiry and co-design processes to ac-
tively engage in problem identification and solution design in three workshops in each region.
The workshop analysis and findings allowed us to design a simple set of questions for current pro-
fessionals and stakeholders, asking them about ways they have addressed the existing challenges
through the semi-structured interview process.
The critical analysis allowed us to identify self-efficacy and skill development, a strong support
system to ensure belonging and safety, and transportation to be the three major ingredients
required for success that address stereotype barriers coming from family and institutional levels,
structural barriers from academic and professional levels, and various safety concerns at the
national level. The elements may appear as known ones, while the systematic exploration of their
impact is important as it can provide direct guidelines for various stakeholders who can positively
impact women in computing. We analyze the findings based on Naila Kabeer’s empowerment
framework [73]. There are other frameworks used in the context of women in computing or
women in STEM that mainly consider the challenges. As this work aims to look at the ingre-
dients for success, we consider Kabeer’s framework - developed in the local context of women
in Bangladesh.
This research work has used the learnings of working with South Asian women using innova-
tive methodological techniques. This work can provide insights for anyone working in Computer
Supported Collaborative Work (CSCW), Human Computer Interaction (HCI), Informa-
tion and Communication Technologies and Development (ICTD) or in the intersectionality
of these areas with other topics. The findings can be used to understand and design solutions for
any socially marginalized community that faces stereotypes or structural challenges.
Specifically, the contribution of our work can be summarized as follows:
— It brings in a 360 degree perspective considering students, professionals, and stakeholders
to understand the current situation of women in computing
— Our work uses fictional inquiry workshops and design workshops to engage the student
participants in understanding their problems with some direction and provides an active
solution design space. The exploration from the workshops is used to explore the viewpoints
of professionals and stakeholders further
— The work identifies three major ingredients for women in computing to succeed: self-efficacy
and skill development, strong social support, and safety transportation through the research
— This work aligns the findings with Naila Kabeer’s empowerment framework to show the
current status of women from a broader perspective
2 Theoretical Perspectives on Women in Computing
Given the extensive body of prior research on women in computing, incorporating perspectives
from gender theory and social psychology offers valuable insights to further enrich our discourse
on this topic. We have tried to have a loose chronological order on how women’s right to
intellectual contribution emerged as a theme. It initiated in Western regions and evolved in other
regions over time.
2.1 The Global Gendered Perception on Intellectual Abilities
This subsection focuses on the global aspect on how intellectual abilities in general, and technology
and computing to be specific, have gendered representation.
Focusing on Gendered Intellect: The initial theoretical debate started looking for evidences
on whether the intelligence of women for scientific thinking and exploration is biological or not.

Freud defined capability of men from psychological and biological abilities were defined as normal,
which women did not have [55]. The thread of exploration continued over years. Over the same
discussion, Eliot searched from a neurological point of view on human brains in her book "Pink
Brain, Blue Brain", showing no significant evidences of gender based intellectual differences [51].
While there are no significant differences in intellectual capabilities based on gender, the question
that arises relates to the social construction of gender differences [81]. The work talks about how,
Everyone “does gender” without thinking about it. It starts at the very beginning when a child is
born and continues forward. The social construction of gender impacts the capabilities and often
perception of capabilities when it stratifies us based on gender differences. As Lorber et al. refer
to it, As a social institution, gender is a process of creating distinguishable social statuses for the as-
signment of rights and responsibilities. And it is observed over time that the intellectual capability
of thinking, exploring and problem solving has been gendered knowingly and unknowingly. The
social factors are further evaluated in the discussion on intersectionality. Crenshaw in her essay
criticizes the tendency to treat Race and Gender as mutually exclusive categories [41]. There are
multi-dimensional factors apart from gender differences coming from race, class or sexual orien-
tation that can further marginalize women or other minority communities [56]. In our work we
also see marginalization of women based on their gender and often justified by the religion and
social norms in Bangladesh.
Gendered Culture of Exclusion around Technology Use: These existing social values get
interlinked with careful creation of a fear element around technology for women, as has been
studied previously [113]. Wyer et al. observed how gender plays a role in the context of science
and technology related fields [137]. Turkle goes back to possible reasons behind gender bias in
technology related fields such as admonishment [134]. It is not uncommon to have gender differ-
ences coming from family as mentioned by Oyewumi [94]. The cultural influence in technology
access is present in South Asian region as well. A study close to our one is discussed in terms of
professional women engineers in the context of India, illustrating the fact of ongoing gender based
technology divide [95]. In recent years, fear is subtle. Society imposed expectations prioritize
male candidates which indirectly impact female students and professionals as has been seen
in Bangladesh [68]. The systematic fear towards technology is not uncommon here along with
other South Asian countries [108]. Our study considers women growing up in the similar cultural
setup and societal perception. However, the women in computing have a better familiarity and
ownership in the technology space continuously fighting various social battles as our study shows.
Stereotype Threat impacting Women in Computing: In many earlier research studies,
stereotype threat has been identified as a significant challenge for women in computing [24, 37, 79].
Stereotype threat is a psychological phenomenon where someone from a marginalized group feels
anxious about confirming a negative stereotype about their social group and this anxiety can ac-
tually hurt their performance in tasks related to the stereotype, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy
[111, 119]. Many prior studies have been conducted on stereotype threat and engagement and
performance of women in computing. Students’ decisions to major in computing are frequently
influenced by their incorrect assumptions that jobs in computer science are extremely technical, ex-
clusive to “nerds,” lonely, and devoid of social connections [30, 40]. Stereotypes exist that computer
scientists are obsessed with technology to the exclusion of other interests [24, 82], lack interper-
sonal skills and socially awkward [24, 112]. Prior work showed that women have less confidence in
their aptitude in computer science than men [24] and women may show less interest in computer
science than men because they believe the discipline is more focused on technology than people
[45]. Reminding women of these negative stereotypes can affect their performance [79]. Negative
stereotypes also affect women’s sense of belonging in classroom [96]. However, positive media
representations [37] can fight against stereotypes and inclusive gender-sensitive environmental

cues in classroom can also influence female participation in computer science [36]. Our work also
found significant negative social stereotypes about the ability of women and desirable professional
roles about women (such as doctors) which we discuss in detail in the section on findings.
Gender and Self Efficacy: Self efficacy - a person’s belief in his capacity to succeed in any
particular situation, has been considered a major predictor of female students plans to study in
computer science and increased chances of pursuing a career in STEM [63, 110]. The term “self-
efficacy,” coined by psychologist Albert Bandura, describes a person’s confidence in their ability to
carry out particular tasks or reach particular objectives [19, 20]. Various factors can improve female
students computing career related self efficacy. Example of such factors can be the influence of role
models, mentoring [59] and seeing other women succeeding [139]. Supportive initiatives such as
integrating computer science in early childhood education boosted self efficacy in women [33]. In-
clusive introductory computer science classrooms with positive student-faculty interactions also
enhanced self efficacy for women and raised their sense of belonging in computing [27]. Research
on computing self-efficacy among women in India showed that Indian women viewed CS as a
women-friendly field, and the findings suggested that depending on culture, Gender, self-efficacy
and computing are built in more diverse ways than is typically acknowledged in prior studies.
Previous studies conducted in Bangladesh also showed that enhancing self-efficacy through cre-
ating a more supportive learning environment is a potential strategy for interventions aimed at
increasing the participation of women in non-traditional disciplines like engineering [106]. Our
research also reveals that while negative stereotypes, a lack of social support, and inadequate
infrastructure affect women in Bangladesh, women with strong social support and self-esteem
frequently overcome these obstacles to pursue higher education and succeed in the workforce.
We have seen our participants using self efficacy as their primary coping mechanism against
obstacles they face in their studies to cover up missed learning opportunities in their learning
spaces.
2.2 The Eastern Feminist Approaches
This subsection focuses on a more eastern perception on how the feminist fight emerged and its
relationship to various threads of the Feminist HCI movement to ensure an inclusive technology
space for women.
South Asian Feminism: The South Asian region shares a colonial history [104]. The societal re-
form during the colonial regime and post-colonial ones around ensuring women’s right continued
with the political changes ongoing at that time [35]. Along with the other social factors, religion
was a strong part of the politics and movement, and it was used vastly during the post-colonial
era [2]. The feminism defined for this region, the South Asian Feminism, has been distinguished
by scholars where it differs from the Western feminist theories and concepts by Spivak [117]. The
South Asian feminist was initiated and inspired by the Western feminist movement and eventually
evolved in its local context [104]. The feminist movement met the nationalistic movement during
its initiation [104]. The nationalistic movements were glorified by the participation of male fight-
ers and supporters, and women’s active roles and passive roles during each political or national
instability remained mostly untold [43, 58].
Islamic HCI and Secular Values in Feminism: Religion has been a factor in dividing the
Indian Subcontinent, and later across India and East Pakistan and West Pakistan [26]. The factor of
religion continued to be the dividing factor across East and West Pakistan [77]. Thus, the national
movement during the inception of Bangladesh asked for secularism as opposed to religious
justification [25]. The feminist movement emerged from the nationalistic movements and sought
secularism and tolerance. Since religion was politicized during the liberation war and has been
heavily used to justify suppression and oppression of women and religious minorities during

the liberation war in 1971, women’s movements placed their positionality against religion-based
decision making which changed over time [74]. This work, based on the values of the feminist
movement of Bangladesh, stands out from religion-based frameworks as proposed by design space
defined by Islamic HCI [66, 88], Hindu HCI [87], religious HCI [103] or parareligious HCI [124]
since religion has been heavily politicized in this region and has been used to separate communities
based on their differences rather than unifying them. Furthermore, in a Muslim majority country, a
religion-based design may exclude the voices of women from the intersectionality of women from
religious minorities, economically disadvantaged ones, or educationally lacking communities.
Feminist HCI and Gender Inclusion: Feminist HCI scholars have played a bold role in
discussing issues regarding women’s rights, incorporation, and involvement. During the third
wave of feminism [21], Feminist HCI community is concerned about inclusion [29]. Our work
relates thematically to the Feminist HCI scholarship as it considers an inclusive space for women
in computing to succeed. This work, focusing on the local context considers design aspects for
inclusion of women with South Asian Feminist concept with our Nationalistic movement focusing
on a specific theory developed incorporating all these background information.
2.3 Naila Kabeer’s Empowerment Framework
While many prior research for Bangladeshi women in computing focused primarily on the chal-
lenges, in our work we want to expand upon the solution drivers. In our findings section, we detail
the relationship between self-efficacy and women’s achievement in Bangladesh with our first se-
cret ingredient. This paper also draws upon the framework for women’s empowerment established
by Naila Kabeer [73] defining empowerment of women. It has 3 interrelated dimensions - resources,
agency and achievement. Resources is a broad term that includes access and as well as future claims
to material, human and social resources. Naila Kabeer’ considers resources to have economic re-
sources as well as social and cultural aspect that governs access to various resources [73]. Agency
is a person’s ability to define and act upon one’s goals. In Naila Kabeer’s definition, “Agency in-
cludes collective, as well as individual, reflection and action. It encompasses analysis, bargaining,
negotiation, deception, manipulation, subversion, resistance, and protest” [73]. Achievements are
the outcomes of choices such as egalitarian decision-making, freedom of movement, etc.
Achievement, as Naila Kabeer mentions, refers to the outcomes measured in terms of well-being
[73]. The framework illustrates elements required for women’s empowerment – a framework that
emphasizes on the solution aspect. We have contextualized our findings to this framework in the
discussion section referring to how this framework shows the gaps towards empowerment in the
current societal context. We discuss our findings upon the context of this framework in Section 6.
3 Related Work
Considering the large body of literature focusing on women in computing, we take a close look at
the status of women in computing in Asian region with a sharper emphasis on Bangladesh with
its regional context.
3.1 Status of Women in Computing in Asia
There is a rich body of literature on the topic of the gender divide in technology, where social
practices, cultural norms, and economic factors play an important role. The number of research
works varies in different countries in Asia as there are a number of studies focusing on women
in computing in regions such as India [57, 62, 99, 131] and Malaysia [56, 80, 84], while there are
limited explorations on regions such as Kuwait [50, 138], Afghanistan [9], or Nepal [115]. For
underrepresented regions, the literature often focuses on general ICT access and training, instead
of women in tertiary education in computing. Some barriers for women are unique to certain

regions, such as those inspired by traditional patriarchal cultures, and religious practices along
with the developing economies of Asian countries [71, 126]. Apart from that, women’s education
is not considered valuable in various cultural contexts, which results in families underinvesting in
their daughter’s education [34].
There is notable diversity in terms of participation of women in computing based on the regional
culture, economic conditions, and status of IT or tech industry. India being in close proximity of
Bangladesh, shows many similarities in its social practices while the IT industry has advanced
significantly. Being attracted to the stability and the well-paid jobs in the IT industry, there is
a wider acceptance from parents and teachers towards the field of computing here [57, 99, 131].
However, there are challenges for women, including underrepresentation, negative stereotypes,
subtle gendered policies in institutes such as strict hostel curfew rules forcing women to limit
their mobility or report at certain times, limited lab facilities, lack of campus security hurt women’s
experiences during educational years in the field of computing [1, 44, 76, 97]. When the workplaces
for IT jobs are considered to be secure, there are physical safety issues, sexual harassment and
unwanted advances during transport, impacting women mostly [62, 131]. The societal pressure of
getting married remains a concern for students during undergraduate years, particularly, during
final years along with the fear that women will be “over-educated” to find a suitable groom if
they pursue higher education such as master’s or Ph.D.; moreover, after marriage, the in-laws
and husbands are often unsupportive [131]. The societal practices remain the same when women
are generally not lacking in confidence in their technical skills, in classroom interactions, male
students are often favored, and male peers engage in discriminatory behaviors such as excluding
women from informal study circles and not giving due credit [62, 131]. Similar gender-specific
prejudices have been visible in many tertiary educational institutes in Bangladesh as contemporary
literature shows along with our exploration in the current studies.
The underrepresentation of women creates barriers in different kinds of environments. For ex-
ample, women may find themselves as the only female participants in their courses or research
groups, leading to feelings of being an outsider and limited interactions with male peers as has
been reported in highly competitive engineering schools of India [62]. Due to the low proportion
of women in computing departments, women may feel isolated and face difficulties seeking help
from male colleagues. Often there is deliberate exclusion of women by men in their groups, limiting
opportunities for interaction and collaboration. Moreover, women researchers experience limited
informal interaction with their advisors compared to men which impacts receiving informal men-
torship, hindering their academic and research growth. Similarly, Hosaka et al. found that female
seniors in engineering programs at national universities in Japan struggled to actively participate
in labs due to being the only woman and lack of encouragement for interaction between male and
female students [65]. Similar concerns are presented by our participants where social expectations
and practices affect participants’ journey in their CS education journey.
However, there are countries that do not have strong representation of women in the ICT field.
The research work focusing on women in computing in Nepal presents concerns such as lack of
gender-sensitive ICT policies, high female poverty, and social perception that ICT careers are more
suited to men hurt the engagement of women [115]. The locations of tele centers are challenging
for women to access computers and the internet easily, specifically during late hours. Rural women
often do not know English resulting in a language barrier. A study on technology access and
usage among women of Afghanistan mentioned while the women have strong familiarity with
technology, they face challenges like inadequate ICT laws for handling online abuse, social restric-
tions on visiting public internet cafes, and family restrictions such as not being able to use one’s
own profile picture or real name in social media [9]. It further shows a regional disparity where
many rural area women are not able to access general education restricting them from technology

access. Many of the resource related challenges are similar for Bangladeshi women from economic
difficulties.
An interesting phenomenon showing a high representation of women in computing is observed
in many Muslim countries such as Malaysia, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia, which have markedly
different gender perceptions around having a career in computing [50, 80, 84, 138]. Computer
science is gender-neutral in these cultures as the studies suggest. Families encourage women to
enroll in computing for diverse reasons, including intrinsic interest, higher income, government
scholarships, and increased job opportunities. There have been examples where fathers have
encouraged their daughters to study computing for financial stability while it has another level
of social safety, having indoor office job opportunities [80, 84]. There has been a deliberate
emphasis from the Government on ensuring a positive perception of women in computing,
optimistic attitude, female role models, and policies on the education of women with a focus on
ICT and quota systems to support Malaysian women in computing [56, 80, 84]. Here the fields
of computing, including software engineering and programming, are considered theoretical and
fit for women [80, 84]. In some Muslim countries, female-only gender-segregated classrooms are
used [15, 50]. Bangladesh, a Muslim-majority country, does not hold such a high representation of
women in computing here. Moreover, the tertiary institutes offer mixed-gender classrooms, unlike
examples showing female-only classrooms. Our work is inspired by the positive approaches that
have worked for women in computing and explores the contextual solution that has worked for
this region.
3.2 Women in Computing in Bangladesh
We provide an insight into the landscape of women’s involvement in computing within
Bangladesh, where we consider both educational and social dimensions through a gender lens.
Exploring the status of women in computing in the Asian region in comparison to Bangladesh
will allow us to contextualize the current problems.
3.2.1 Women’s Social and Educational Landscape of Bangladesh. The social and educational con-
texts of women in Bangladesh are important to understand the current barriers and opportunities
for women in computing.
Bangladesh is considered a country that emphasizes female education [48], showing equal
representation at primary levels where the number of female students gradually drop in higher
classes [17, 18]. However, the social practices impact women’s development where concerns like
child marriage and early marriage take place [125]. The challenges exacerbate with infrastructural
limitations like lack of childcare support are present [127]. Moreover, the patrilineal descent where
a lineage group is influenced by male members and patrilocal residence where women move to
live with their husbands and relatives are practiced here, impacting women’s decision making and
independence [120]. Here, the father or male member of the house is considered to be the head
of household, being the income generator who dominates decision-making [22]. The patriarchal
practices impact the access and exposure to technology as the recent studies have shown
[108, 109, 123].
There is gender disparity from the perspective of technology access and exposure. A study
exploring 25 countries that considered Bangladesh showed that women experience ICT usage and
access barriers in developing countries [130]. The challenges cover infrastructural ones impacting
low resource communities such as weak infrastructure impacting internet access, power supply
and communication system. The challenges affect women more since the social constraints impact
women to reach out to these resources such as a publicly available internet access point. It places
women and other marginalized communities to have a lower access and exposure to technology

which makes them easy target of technology based abuse and harassment [108, 109]. Conse-
quences of such abusive experience include emotional harm and reputation damage [91, 108, 109].
Moreover, women are expected to behave in certain ways online, otherwise, there is a possibility to
be negatively represented which results in limiting access or identity or expression [3, 91, 108, 109].
In the gendered positionality based on the Global Gender Gap Report 2023, Bangladesh ranks
first in South Asia in terms of gender parity (scoring 72.2%) and ranks 59th globally [129]. A close
look at the educational attainment sub-index reveals a persistent gap in enrollment in tertiary edu-
cation [129]. It shows the female literacy rate for the 15+ age group to be similar to the male group
being 73% and 78.2% for females and male respectively. However, there is a high dropout rate in the
transition from higher secondary to tertiary level education, showing around 22.72% of students
dropping out after higher secondary education. The current tertiary education gross enrollment
ratio (GER) is 18.66% of the total population. ICT education starts early in Bangladesh from the 6th
grade. 79.65% of colleges have computer labs. However, there is a disparity depending on the insti-
tute such as only 16.27% of the madrasa have computer labs. At the tertiary level, there are 164 uni-
versities offering tertiary education in Bangladesh, while the female representation is low, as only
37.58% of total students and 29.79% of total teachers are women. There is a limitation of data as en-
rollment of computing specifically was not addressed in Bangladesh Education Statistics 2022 [18].
This high dropout rate impacts the proportion of women in computer science and related fields.
Gender-based social practices and barriers such as child marriage, early motherhood, and violence
against women, impact women’s drop of higher education which further impacts the lower repre-
sentation of women in job sectors [93]. The participation of female students shows promise, as re-
cent work suggested higher enrollment of female students at the tertiary level [69]. Although there
is an increase in number of female students, the number remains low in STEM fields. There are a
number of identified reasons, including societal perceptions, poor infrastructure, and prejudice.
As mentioned before, the Government of Bangladesh has introduced gender-sensitive policies
to increase female enrollment. It has shown significant increase in female students at Primary
and Secondary education levels. The policy ensures free education till grade 8 for female students
as opposed to male students being supported till class 5 in government schools. Several initiatives
have been taken to increase the participation of women in education by the Bangladesh govern-
ment such as several programs aimed at enhancing women’s literacy, provision of free education
for girls up to the university level and offering stipends for girls attending secondary schools
in rural areas [14, 102]. Additionally, to meet the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development
Goals (SDG), particularly the goal of “quality education”, there are initiatives such as provision of
free textbooks, programs to decrease dropout rates, and making ICT education mandatory from
grade 6 to 12, and so on [14]. Moreover, the“Digital Bangladesh” initiative aimed to promote ICT
accessibility in all areas starting in 2008 [92].
It shows great possibilities with areas to improve to ensure an increase in the number of women
with technology access towards pathways to having more women in computing.

We have considered research work taking place in last eight years that has considered
Bangladeshi women in computing such as IT, ICT, Computer Science, Computer Science and En-
gineering, and so on, as presented in Table 1. We closely analyzed these works along with other
related research to understand the current status of women in computing. The studies have taken
place in traditional interview methods including surveys, one to one interviews, focus group dis-
cussions across students, professionals, and various stakeholders [5, 6, 8, 68, 105, 121, 128]. We
discuss the challenges and solution approaches proposed in the contemporary literature.
A categorization of the challenges women in computing face shows that the problems are com-
ing from several major factors. There is a stereotype barrier about a women’s role and ability that
hampers women in computing: it creates an acceptance problem of professionals who may have
to work long hours or have to consider challenging responsibilities while such perception creates
a lack of confidence among young learners. For example, the work by Iftekhar et al. shows female
students considering themselves to be “Less competent” compared to their male peers [68]. There
are structural challenges in institutions including lack of space in laboratory, poor internet access
and limited equipment availability for female students. It is prominent for the students who are
residing in residential halls.
For example, there are specialized labs but access was not open for female students; in public
universities female residential halls had stricter return time and rules for female students prevent-
ing them from group discussion or group learning activities [5]. The stereotype around women
also hampers their performances in laboratory based group learning environments as the studies

show [68]. It shows that the challenges are not discrete; they are inter-related, impacting women
from various dimensions. The challenges for women continue in their workplaces where there
are reports of various difficult situations.. The ongoing stereotype exacerbates the problem where
recent work has shown an example where a high official has referred to women working in IT
sector to have “Lower intelligence” in a public discussion forum [5]. It shows an alarming picture
of how women in computing are perceived and how the demeaning comments about women’s
intelligence is considered socially acceptable. Apart from the existing challenges that take place
in families and institutions, there is a broader set of security and transportation related problems
that impact women in general and hamper their mobility and growth entirely. The ongoing cul-
ture of abuse and harassment towards women in physical spaces as well as cyber space and lack
of punishment for such incidents provide a snapshot of the current scenario [13, 108, 109, 122].
The contemporary study shows a lack of safety and transportation as a major barrier for women
in computing, particularly for them to pursue a career. A study shows how a woman was sexu-
ally abused during her extensive training sessions by her mentors and she considered it to be her
own fault that impacted her wellbeing for a while as presented in the research [6]. There are im-
pacts of these infrastructural limitations on women and women in computing. Moreover, there is
a lack of support networks and mentoring that could collectively uplift the community of women
in computing as the studies show. There are discrete networks at smaller scales but there is still a
requirement to have a better support system that is sustainable beyond institutions or individual
efforts. The solution approaches upon categorization are proposed or tried out by the researchers
as the studies have shown in Table 1. The solutions range from creating comfortable learning and
working spaces (e.g., suggesting female-only classrooms or similar activities), creating supportive
networks and mentoring, having ways to address abuse and safety problems at the institution level
as well as the national level (e.g., through constitutional rights and policies), and so on.
However, there is an existing gap in the current set of researchers where we tried to contribute
to complement the existing body of work. The current research methods focus on direct inquiry
while we have used some indirection in the goal to understand the intensity or feelings regarding
the existing challenges which could enrich the body of research and strengthen our effort towards
solution strategies. We also consider the solution approach being actively designed by the women
in computing along with analysis provided by the researchers in our work, unlike existing works.

4.2 Series of Workshops with Tertiary Level Students
In the effort to create a safe sharing space with non-verbal communication methods, there was
sharing through writing and drawing to express the ongoing challenges women in computing
faced. There were two workshops involving writing letters to fictional characters, referred to as
Fictional Inquiry (FI) workshops, to explore the challenges. The final workshop was one where
participants engaged in designing solutions through a co-design workshop. These are presented
in Table 3.
As mentioned before, Fictional Inquiry (FI) was used to provide a comfortable communica-
tion space using two different fictional characters to “bypass existing socio-cultural structures in
a given practice” [47]. FI uses simple ‘props’ to create partially fictional scenarios and artifacts
to let the participants explore the world through a fictional lens which assists in coordinating or
prompting the imaginations of the participants [46, 47, 70]. Fictional inquiry-based solutions have
been used in different contexts, e.g., education setting for co-designing with preschoolers [23],
reimagining museum experiences [70], designing city games with marginalized communities [46],

The qualities of support are retrieved from existing literature focusing on women in computing

and specific solution-related responses. We found overarching themes around barriers women
in computing faced, along with the analysis on elements that were essential to success for them.

5 The Analytical Process of Understanding Successful Women in Computing
The study aims to explore the elements that are required for women in computing to succeed
considering the ongoing challenges present in the country. In order to define the successful
women in technology, a group of researchers collaboratively worked to design the personal that
represents professional women. The collaborative discussion revealed that successful women
are those who were able to work in their own fields comprising of software engineers, academic
faculty and graduate students, and are able to make independent decisions around it. The persona
design process involved an analytical exploration of the study findings around what were the
key elements needed for success for women in computing under various conditions. For example,
the challenges of married professionals appeared to be different from unmarried ones. The
construction of persona and categorization was done in a collaborative manner. We describe the
personas and its design process in the following subsections.

5.1 Persona Design Process
The persona design process was based on the representation participant pool of Professionals
working in the field of Computing. The major factor to define the success as a parameter of women
in computing relied on being able to pursue a career in respective field that was defined from the
discussions of the study participants and stakeholders. The lower number of women pursuing a
career in the field of computing was the motivating factor to understand the scenarios of women
already pursuing their careers along with the ones towards that pathway.
The persona design process allowed the researchers to humanize the problems into imaginary
characters representing a broader community as a whole. A persona provides a fictional name,
identity that has certain pain points and opportunities with a defined goal to achieve. Our persona
design process created the analytical framework to explore and categorize challenges hampering
women in computing to achieve their goals, which in turn is needed to identify necessary elements
coming from the entire pool of successful participants.
The representation of the persona followed using baseline criteria using the common features
from that pool of participants and picking the challenges as a combination of challenges the group
faced. For example, the group of participants working as software engineers being from a similar
age group had similar expectations from jobs while the challenges they faced varied based on their
location and social context. Since the work aims to explore the challenges and possible strategies
that worked in those contexts, we used a combination of challenges accumulated from different
software engineer participants. The persona represented the early career participants which re-
flected the participants being in the professional field. The persona design process was based en-
tirely on the study findings that were synthesized further to identify key factors towards success
as defined previously. It involved categorizing the factors from a top down manner, starting with
the views of the professionals and stakeholders, and finally mapping them to the experiences of
the learners. It was a process of trying to find the leak from the leaky pipeline where learners drop
out to become successful career persons.
Two researchers involved in all the interviews worked on the skeleton persona design and
the rest joined the discussion on finalizing it. It went through a two-phase process where in the
first phase, the groups were selected and the main features were extracted. In the second phase,
the persona was developed based on categorical information. The first author was in charge of
creating the hand-drawn faces reflecting on previous experiences and committing the possibility
of misrepresentation that could happen if openly available photos were used. It was done in a
collaborative manner. The persona design and development were finalized on handwritten cards
rather than an electronic soft copy as the tangible card was easy to share for follow-up discussion.
The entire process is presented in the Appendix.
5.2 The Representative Persona
The representative personas are considered to be early career women in computing, all within the
first ten years after completion of undergraduate studies. This was to relate to the leaks that take
place from the transition from tertiary level studies towards the career path. The software engineer,
graduate student, and academic professional are considered and two are considered to be married
while two are unmarried. We present the set of persona designs in the following subsections.
5.2.1 Persona: Software Engineer. The software engineer persona, named Nina Saha, as can be
seen in Figure 3(a) shows an unmarried person who joined a local company in Bangladesh. As an
emerging professional, she wishes to reach a higher position in the industry.
Nina has a supportive surrounding – a family and friend circle that respects her decisions. The
support circle also includes a mentor who guides her well in the industry environment. The design

The current work culture in software firms, along with a lack of adequate knowledge about

Young software developers like Nina face professional struggles along with the social ones. In
the professional space, often female developers are not given challenging projects and women are
not recognized for their contributions in many cases. There is also the case of being scrutinized
constantly by peers or others in the industry as presented in the personal design.

Sadia faces various social challenges as she lives with her in-laws. Her in-laws make conscious

her job. The participants in academia shared their flexibility while the married participants shared
about their struggle to manage in-laws and family for higher studies. This persona also struggles
to manage time to pursue higher studies abroad.
Sadia wishes to pursue higher studies since she has an excellent academic profile. However, her
ongoing responsibilities make it hard to reach out and extend professional collaborations. The

5.2.3 Persona: Graduate Student. A number of tertiary level students wished to pursue their
