Rahma and Mariam as a married persona and an unmarried persona.
The personas receive great social support since the decision to study abroad requires support
from immediate family. In the close knit structure of Bangladesh, the support from extended
family and influential family members also become important. The married graduate students
received support from families as in a majority of the cases their spouses accompanied them as
presented in the case of Rahma. While there was no family or societal pressure to get married, the
participants struggled about the comments and expectations of expanding their families. A very
personal decision of a couple becomes the affair of the entire family in a Bangladeshi household.
The concern relating to the ticking of biological clocks to have a baby also impacts the individual.
The great support from families is an important factors for the unmarried graduate students. The
unmarried persona, on the other hand, struggles about meeting new people who are not afraid to
accept her as a smart woman. There is increasing family pressure to get married, accompanied by
personal worries about finding the right person. However, the social struggle remains that reflects
societal expectations and impacts the immediate families of the participants directly, as the study
participants shared. The unmarried participants shared about the constant social pressure for
getting married, while the married participants shared about the similar pressure of conceiving
babies. The very personal decision of having a life partner or having a baby is a societal concern
in Bangladesh’s current social structure.
The societal perceptions impact the performances of the participants as has been reflected in
the personas. The social pressure creates a sense of failure or not doing well enough among the
participants and is reflected in the persona design. Wellbeing and self-acceptance are hampered
easily by society, which has direct and indirect impacts on women in general, along with women
in computing.

6 The First Necessary Ingredient to Improve Skills and Self-Efficacy
The first ingredient for success, suggested unanimously by the participants, appears as a way to
improve self-efficacy through knowledge and skills improvement. These requirements are not easy
to achieve since there are gender-specific barriers and social-cultural practices impacting women’s
skill development that hampers self-efficacy as a result.
A critical analysis from this study allows us to see it as the extra effort women are required
to provide for existing perceived skill gaps coming from gender stereotypes. The stereotype bar-
riers arise from societal perceptions of what women can do or are allowed to do. The existence
of stereotypes about women and women’s roles have been discussed in contemporary research
work focusing on women in computing [5, 68]. Previous work showed how women in computing
were considered to be less competent compared to their male peers [68]. The stereotype continued
in the workplace where officials refer to professional women in computing to be less intelligent [5].
It shows that the social stereotype about women’s capabilities and intelligence impacts the per-
ception towards them. Moreover, it shows the social acceptance of sharing such a mindset about
women or, specifically, towards women in computing.
The view towards this first ingredient varies across participants. The professional participants
discussed the importance of skill acquisition in the professional world to address various stereo-
types about women’s abilities. They emphasized preparing oneself to address negative perceptions
and ensuring a spot in the workplace to reduce humiliation. The study shows the presence of such
humiliation towards women is common in the tech industry. These participants accepted the soci-
etal challenges and referred to their workaround in their presence of them. On the other hand, the
student participants mostly focused on places where gender disparity impacts their knowledge and
skill development process. These participants asked for gender-neutral upbringing and learning
environment to ensure they are able to acquire the necessary skills since these are affected by the
stereotypes around women, accompanied by various structural barriers for women. The student
participants did not want to comply with societal values and were eager to challenge the ongoing
barriers to seeking equality in their learning spaces.
6.1 Personal Development as a Coping Mechanism from Stereotype Bias
The professional participants all clearly prioritized skill development as the key element required
for success. There were varied viewpoints across professionals - some considered skill develop-
ment to be one’s responsibility while a majority referred to its importance to handle continuous
judgement from others. This viewpoint was entirely different from students’ perspective since the
students emphasized on existing learning barriers rather than handling the knowledge gap. On
the other hand, the professionals talked about filling up the skill gap or knowledge gap regardless
of previous barriers to ensure entry to the professional world.
It clearly showed the importance of remaining skillful in the face of stereotype biases. A pro-
fessional participant S5 shared how she was humiliated in her first interview when she paused
to answer a basic programming question. The interviewer questioned her ability in a humiliating
manner: “ .. you don’t even know this?”. She had to take a short break before she was able to prepare
for the second interview. She mentioned feeling extremely low, blaming herself for delaying her
answer, and she was traumatized to turn blank in future interviews. She made sure she was well
prepared, emphasizing skill development. The participant did not bother to imagine a welcom-
ing interview board for women. Rather, she suggested future job seekers prepare well to develop
their skills. In the local tech industry, the environment is biased against women, as participants
from the software industry suggested. Two participants from academia shared about their initial
careers in software firms which they left for being continuously judged and monitored about their

abilities. Participant S6 shared how a mistake from women is seen as a lack of skill, unlike their
male colleagues. It is paired with insulting comments shared jokingly or in harsh ways. For exam-
ple, a participant working in software industry, S6, shared about it:
Sometimes some developers are very aggressive. If you can’t do something, they will
ask “how did you come this far without knowing anything?”
Professional participants working as faculties clearly shared how gender discriminatory roles are
given to female faculty where they are often given responsibilities of mundane jobs with lower
visibility. Similarly, the professional participants as graduate students faced direct or subtle gen-
der bias in their academic institutions in Bangladesh and beyond. It shows the presence of strong
gender stereotype beyond our own socio-cultural barriers. A participant joining a prestigious grad-
uate school for PhD shared how she was looked down upon on her skills and abilities which she
had to prove multiple times over the years:
I did feel some gender bias even as a Stanford student. In my research lab, I had
collaborators and mentors. They had kind of a preconception against me, that I’m a
female, I come from a developing country, I must not be very well trained. They were
trying to control me, where they would try to modify language. I didn’t feel good
about it.
Moreover, the professionals referred to extracurricular and co-curricular activities to enhance skills
as their own responsibilities. They clearly shared their ways of acquiring skills. Many of these par-
ticipants shared about personal skill development through curricular and co-curricular activities
along with the self-development process. Many of them shared that academic and professional
clubs, such as the IEEE Student Chapter, ACM Student Chapter, and Competitive Programming
Club, are great starting points for skill development beyond classroom learning. Many of the par-
ticipants strongly proposed the self-development process. For example, participant S4, a software
engineer, shared about using a mantra of Doing it anyway in the face of an obstacle. Similar ideas
were shared by participants working as faculty members, such as S3 and S4. Another participant
shared her way of handling it as follows:
I focus on practice. I got better with practice. I keep watching tutorials, reading articles,
clearing my concepts, and seeing results, and then I get more feedback and confidence.
It has been 2 years, and I’m more confident now. Instead of putting time in tension,
it’s much better to go straight to action. I also follow the quote, “Do it anyway.” I used
to be afraid that I couldn’t do it, it was taking a lot of time, etc. But now I tell myself
to do it anyway. Regardless of how I feel, I just tell myself to do it anyway. I got this
growth by practicing more. - S8, Female, Software Engineer, urban region, Dhaka.
It was clear that the skill development requirements were a coping mechanism for the partici-
pants to address the stereotype bias. The stereotype paired with abusive expression that is socially
acceptable affected the participants who had to put the effort to improve themselves rather than
questioning the system.
6.2 Support to Study in the Field of Computing
The student participants discussed their desire to have a change in the mindset of parents and
surrounding people to accept women in the field of Computing and Engineering. The learning and
skill development as an ingredient for success requires approval from close surroundings such as
parents and guardians to start the tertiary level education, as the study shows.
The participants wished for easy entry into computer science and engineering or related fields,
which was not the case for many of them. Their choices were influenced by the stereotype about

what women should study. Medicine was a societally agreed upon field for women. It creates entry
barriers for many female students studying sciences. Moreover, once one studies computing be-
yond family choices, the participants face inherent pressure to prove themselves right. A student
participant, P30, shared the situation in her words: At least from Bangladesh’s perspective, many
families want their daughters to become doctors if they are letting their female children pursue higher
education. I am not even referring to families who suppress their daughters’ career aspirations, their
situation is even more challenging and distressing which is beyond my imagination. A student par-
ticipant P24, in her letter to Oporajita, shared the social pressure with intense emotion about this
influence as:
We still face a lot of challenges, specially, in engineering, not a lot of girls choose this
sector due to our social misleading thoughts. In our society, everybody imagines a
successful girl as a doctor, when someone hears that we want to be engineers, people
don’t encourage that a lot. Girls are not still free to choose their careers. I have seen
a lot of my friends who do not prepare themselves for engineering just for this social
issue. As a result, very few girls are seen in our university which is another challenge
for this engineering female students.
Moreover, the family preference and expectations towards their daughter’s study field places an
emotional burden on the learners willing to pursue computing. The study shows that participants
studying computing beyond their family will encounter internal pressure of proving themselves
right and continuous fear of failing, starting from the dreams to entering the program. For example,
the student participant P50, shared her thoughts in her letter to Oporajita clearly:
Speaking for myself, one of the challenges I encountered was getting into an Engi-
neering University. My father wanted me to become a doctor because, according to
our society, it was considered more suitable for girls. However, I wanted to explore
myself as an engineering student. I had to endure the disapproval of many relatives,
and I was afraid of potential embarrassment if I didn’t get accepted. But with sheer
determination and a stroke of fate, I made it here, and I’m happy with how things
worked out. - P50, female, student, sub-urban region, Chottogram.
The student participants engaged in designing solution approaches during the design work-
shops. They emphasized mostly on addressing gender bias in learning space as well as at home.
There were suggestions such as conducting gender-awareness workshops or ways to decrease bias
from participants P50 as Implement awareness programs and training to recognize and challenge un-
conscious biases in the workplace.- P50 and P49 seeking By providing evidence, sharing success stories,
and addressing systemic barriers, we can create an environment that promotes gender equality and
diversity in the field of computers. A participant shared her thoughts in more details as follows:
We need to encourage other women around us and teach men to restrain gender biases.
We need to train more women in the industry so that women can have the opportunity
to prove themselves before we move on to normalizing such jobs for both genders. -
P44, female, student, sub-urban, Chottogram.
The study shows how gender biases implicitly and explicitly impact career choices and the
journey toward it for women in computing.
6.3 Enabling Learning Environment
The student participants wished to have a gender-neutral learning environment. The learning
process was affected by the stereotype bias of teachers along with many structural limitations.

Participants shared how academic faculty members’ bias about female students’ intellectual abil-
ity hampered the confidence of female students and their learning process. The comments about
teachers came mostly from fictional inquiry-based letter responses. Several participants, mostly
outside the capital city, shared their gendered learning experiences. Some participants shared fac-
ulties referring to programming skills not being important for female students. Moreover, there
were discussions on the varied capabilities of female learners. A student participant, P22, shared
about the gendered perception of faculties about learning capabilities:
They think we girls have less analytical skills; we are only capable of remembering
things, not implementing or doing something practical. This type of mentality is also
noticeable in our respected teachers.
Another student participant, P45, resonated with similar experiences, saying that she was underes-
timated as a female learner, pushing her more towards theoretical learning rather than hands-on
skills. A student participant, P47, shared the case clearly Some Male teachers do not provide proper
care to the (female) students. I have faced this problem. It showed how the participant felt not be-
ing cared enough, which is not desirable. Another student participant P44, shared in her letter to
Oporajita about faculty bias about skills as follows:
I still have teachers in my classroom who underestimate my ability in lab work. And,
on most days, I am tired of being labeled as a “female” engineer, not just an “Engineer”.
P44, female, student, sub-urban region, Chottogram.
As the study explores, the structural barriers in the learning space impact the female students
more. For example, female students are often pushed away from active learning in a constrained
learning space, particularly in laboratory-based learning spaces. The situation is similar in urban
and non-urban universities, where the number of hardware setups is limited.
The limited resources and space scarcity reinforce laboratory-based learning to take place in
large groups. In many cases, the male students dominate the lab classes; female students, being a
minority in groups, often do not actively participate in the process. If a number of male students
dominate the area, female students hesitate to ask for their space in laboratories, remaining passive
learners. It hampers their skill levels as the participants shared while the perception from faculty
members varies from the learners. The academic faculty members refer to the passive learning
process of female students as disengagement, as a faculty participant S5 shared,
Female students are often better at math at the HSC level. But it’s the lab where there
seems to be a gap. Developing hands-on skills where the real gap keeps happening. IT
education is practical and hands-on, which women lack.
The student perspective was different, sharing about the barrier coming from social settings as
student participant P53 shares: Many times girls don’t participate properly in labs or group work
because of shyness. A student participant P49 in her letter to Oporajita explained her experience in
detail as follows:
In our 1st/2nd semester, we completed some labs based on electrical experiments.
We faced unequal opportunities for advancements or leadership roles during those
labs. Most of the time, all male students successfully did their experiments with
the teacher’s help. However, we, females, failed to do our lab work as a minority
group. All male students crowded together during those experiments and completed
their experiments as a team. But we are a minority team, and we failed to enter that
crowd, hear the teacher’s lecture, and so on. - P49, female, student, sub-urban region,
Chottogram.

Fig. 5. Location of female hostels in suburban campuses.
At the infrastructure level, there are other limitations hampering learning and exploration.
The female students from suburban regions residing in residential halls shared how the secured
locations of the female-halls hamper the internet access severely. The faculty and academic
administrators refer to ensuring the safety of their female students making sure their residents are
placed on the campus where outsiders cannot enter easily. Figure 5 shows the locations of female
hostels being further from the main campus, as the participants shared. Furthermore, the evening
rules requiring female students (not applicable for male students) to return to the hall by sunset
also limits the learning since they are not allowed to access the on-campus lab resources or join
group discussions. A participant, P24, shared it as:
Still, women have to be back in the residential area very early time, after sunset, though
they have work outside.
Moreover, structural barriers impact female students’ learning process. Participants shared their
difficulties in entering co-curricular activities, such as joining a programming club. For example,
participant P11 shared, The club claims to help sharpen the programming skills of the members, which
is why I tried to get into the club for 3 consecutive semesters, but due to my lack of skills, I never even
made it through the preliminary levels. I notice a lot of cliques on campus (in my department) that
discuss things like coding, competitions, projects, etc, but sadly enough, I don’t ever see any girls in
these cliques. In a few cases, the labs were inaccessible considering the evening rules designed
for female residential students to return to their halls by sunset, limiting their access as student
participant P36 shares,
Although our ACM lab remains open 24 hours for practice sessions and programming-
related activities, we (female students) are unable to access the facilities during night
time.
As a design solution, student participants shared about ensuring gender equality from parents
and teachers starting at an early age, shared by participants P18 and P22 from Rajshahi, as can be
seen in Figure 6. The solutions suggested in the Figure addressed gender bias mainly. It strongly
focuses on gender-neutral teachers and parents to ensure fairness in classrooms as well as at home.
In the close-knit South Asian society, where generational hierarchy is important, addressing the

Fig. 6. Solutions suggested for parents and teachers through an awareness process.
limitations of parents or teachers is not common. Unlike previous studies conducted regionally to
address this problem (e.g., [5, 6, 6–8] etc.), the FI based letter writing followed by design sessions
provided such discussions in the form of solution design. The solutions in Figure 6(a) show a
flowchart of training required for a teacher, observing a teacher through demo classes; an inability
to meet gender-neutral teaching will not allow the teacher to teach a class. It is a strong point
to refer to what might be missing from existing classrooms. The faculty are not trained towards
such gender neutrality and their behavior impacts the learners intensely, as our study showed. The
solution in Figure 6(b) shows therapy and awareness sessions designed for parents and teachers
to ensure gender-neutral behavior. The solution approaches show the requirement to consider
gender sensitivity training. It also shows severe gender bias in families and educational institutes
that might have discouraged other potential women in computing.
It showed that the student participants were eager to address the existing challenges with pas-
sion and care, considering the impacts it had on them.
7 The Second Essential Ingredient Related to the Sense of Belonging
The study participants unanimously shared the importance of a support network, awareness about
it, and mentoring facilities from professional bodies as well as in social circles. The professional par-
ticipants mentioned the presence of a support system and the requirement to create one, if such
a system does not exist. The study showed clearly that a strong support system is required for
women in computing to navigate their learning path as well as their professional journeys. Partic-
ipants sometimes received support from family, friends, social circles, and professional networks.
On the other hand, a number of participants mentioned compensating for the lack of support from
one sector with the other. It must be noted that the professionals as participants referred to the sup-
port system beyond the academic domain, while the student participants discussed mostly support
from families.

The professional participants have placed realistic limitations where one may face adversities
in her immediate family, in-laws, or professional circle. They asked about ensuring one positive
network to navigate the difficulties and mentioned the temporal nature of such adversities. For
example, there are examples of a participant facing reservations from her in-laws about her de-
cision to study abroad, which became possible by the support from her mother and colleagues.
The disagreement of in-laws subsided as she received full funding and a scholarship from a pres-
tigious university. The student participants, on the other hand, mentioned existence of various
social-cultural challenges and hoped for a positive network to support them. We discuss them in
the following subsections.
7.1 Requirement of an Immediate Strong Support System
A few participants shared about receiving great support from family but not from professional
circles, while few others mentioned the opposite scenario, but all agreed upon the requirement of
a support system to navigate the journey as a woman in computing.
The support from immediate families has a direct influence on participants. Participant S13,
pursuing her PhD shared about not receiving much support from her parents, while it got easier
after she got married. She received great support from her spouse. She explained how joining the
same university made it easier as It was great that my husband and I had the same desire to pursue
higher education, and luckily, we got admission to the same university. Another Ph.D. student, S14,
who came for higher studies before getting married, shared about the strong position of her mother
towards higher studies to be her driving force as:
Ammu (mother) asked me to apply abroad. She said, why would you waste time stay-
ing here? She did not allow any negative comments to reach me.
As the study showed, the support is important and relevant since the immediate family often
creates pressure to get married, which is difficult to ignore. It was an overarching issue across
all the participants. It impacts individuals as the discussion of marriage often refers to women’s
marriageable age along with the biological body clock of having babies. It creates social pressure for
getting married, placing the responsibility on individuals who wish to pursue a career. Participant
P51 shared her thoughts during the design session as The problem is that family pressure inhibits
female students from getting a good education, which results in a lower percentage of women working
in computing. Early marriage and dowries are typical barriers that prevent women from participating..
Another participant P40, portrayed more on how the marriage and the preferences of in-laws after
marriage impact the exploration: Also not everyone gets the same support and assistance from their
family. Sometimes early marriage makes some of them give up on their dream if the in-laws are not
that supportive of continuation of studies. Their own family can sometimes oppose the pursuit of their
dream. Participant P23, in her letter to M3, shared how the parent’s preferences impact the journey
as follows:
Again, if women get enough support from family and society, they will be able to give
enough time and will be able to be serious about their work. In Bangladesh, parents’
ultimate goal is to get married to their daughter to an established person rather than
support their daughter in establishing her career. And in the case of marriage, most
Bangladeshi men consider looks as a primary standard. -P23, female, student, urban,
Rajshahi.
The challenges continue as one progresses toward a professional life, as the study shows. The
participants working in the academic and software industry as well as in graduate studies all have
shared about the pressure they have faced from families, extended families, and beyond. Societal

involvement interferes with the very personal decisions of having a child. For example, a partici-
pant continuing as a graduate student shared:
Current obstacles I’m facing is that career is not the main. They are talking about my
age. I kind of agree. I’m not getting younger. I’m likely to get more complications in
future. If I do want to extend the family may be its a good idea to start now. But I’m
very busy all the time. Right now I’m not mentally prepared for being a parent. They
keep telling me that even if I want I will not get a family later. - S13, female, Phd
student, USA.
It showed the impact on the wellbeing on individuals thus having a supporting immediate family
to be a major requirement for success.
7.2 Sustainable Support through Professional Network and Awareness Generation
The support is required in the academic and professional environment as the study participants
from student community as well as professional communities shared.
The student participants shared about the requirement of support since there are times when
female students feel excluded. The religious justification not to cooperate with peers are accepted
in classrooms as the study shows. The exclusion of female peers affects their learning as well
as their confidence as a number of participants shared. A participant shared the impact of such
behavior in her words as follows:
Due to religious attitudes or social norms, many boys do not want to participate prop-
erly in class activities with classmates of the opposite sex. In this case, various group
activities or discussions are hindered and girls lag behind. -P53, female, student, sub-
urban region, Chottogram.
The impact on students is higher when the negligence or exclusion comes from the direct teach-
ers. The participants did not discuss about their teachers much verbally, it came mostly through
the letters and design solutions. A student participant P20, in her letter to Oporajita shared her
feelings about this experience:
Some teachers behave weirdly with girls. Some religious teachers don’t want to com-
municate with girls in the class. This is true that for religious purpose, it’s fine. But we
went there to study. If teachers don’t want to communicate with us, it will be tough
for us to study there.
On the other hand, in the tech industry, some of the professional participants shared about
the benefit of having mentors to guide them through this environment. The positive culture
of mentoring junior software engineers was shared by most of the participants working in
software industry with two exceptions. A participant S6 working in software industry shared,
Our superviser was very good to new trainees. If I couldn’t do something the supervisers and the
mentors helped with onboarding. A participant pursuing higher studies, S15 also shared the intense
support from her mentor. The participants who are currently students shared about the positive
role of mentoring and support network strongly. The requirement to increase awareness around
support system was also mentioned here. The student participants, mostly, in their letters to M3,
shared about support culture requirements in the job sector. A student participant, P28, shared it
in her letter to M3 as follows:
To address the challenges faced by women, it is important to consider the systemic
barriers they encounter. These barriers include unconscious biases, gender stereotypes,
limited access to opportunities, and a lack of representation and Mentorship.

Fig. 7. (a, b) Solution design promoting women. (c) Young female role model using computers.
The student participants laid out a detailed solution through design workshops where the net-
work, mentoring, support system, and awareness generation were rigorously discussed.
The participants referred clearly to awareness generation on the impact and achievements of
current women in computing, which in turn could create a better social support system for them.
There were multiple solution designs around building strong mentoring platforms, highlighting
achievements of women in computing, and media’s positive representation of women in the soft-
ware industry. A student participant P44 in her design workshop strongly shared how the aware-
ness can influence the caregivers and support them throughout the journey as follows:
Designing Social Media Platform in a way when women achievements in technology
are exposed. In terms of perception, Social media plays powerful role. To publish the
motivational, spiritual, women success, Cultural influence, and achievements content
in social media for parents so that they are motivated for their daughter’s education
in science relevant (Strong) subjects to play a vital role in job for future. Not to show
the negative content in media eg. Women are vulnerable. As parents are too much in-
fluenced by social media, Expose more women to portfolios who are doing computing
work all over the world. Its can be done by Building ALGORITHM where women’s
positive energy contents should be highlighted.
The participants have designed multiple solutions to portray women in computing during the
design session as Figure 7 shows; a web-based solution to portray women in Figures 7(a) and 7(b)
and a female role model in a popular cartoon character using computers in (c), respectively. The
solutions designed by participants show different ways to ensure support for women in comput-
ing. In Figure 7(a), a detailed slow chart-type diagram shows several elements: it discusses the
role of media such as Facebook posts, entertainment based outlets like drama, movies, cartoons;
followed by ways to generate interest in computing by exposing them through books and tech
devices; that is paired by teachers’ and parents’ training; once one entered the computing job- en-
suring safety and equal salary; and finally, providing a supporting environment through mentoring,

care - increasing opportunity and adequate salary structure. The solution provided in Figure 7(b)
shows awareness generation through a web interface that highlights achievements of women in
computing, e.g., showing the winner of International Olympiad of Informatics (IOI), celebrat-
ing a networking event titled Ada Lovelace (that has taken place in the past three years [8]), free-
lancing opportunities and suggestions for gifts focused on maths to encourage the younger genera-
tion in technical fields. The final solution presented here in Figure 7(c) shows a popular role model
Meena, designed by the UN towards gender neutrality for upbringing girls in South Asia, to start
using a computer. The solutions clearly indicated gaps in the support system the participants iden-
tified. The solutions strongly show the societal awareness as a major component emphasizing more
on immediate families. It also shows enablers where the girls at early age can access technology
without any restrictions. The design workshop has enabled the participants to explore the required
elements for a better environment for women in computing. The paper- and pen-based design ses-
sions allowed participants to use various forms of solution design - a technical flowchart, that is
commonly used in computer science-based problem solving or fast sketches to place the thoughts
on paper or an imagination that shapes up later through a computer aided model of Meena. The
forms of expressions and varied problem solving directions also allowed elements of freedom
for participants.
8 The Final Important Ingredient of Seeking Transportation and Safety
Every single participant shared about transportation and safety as a barrier hampering women in
general, regardless of their age, gender, location, or profession. It was an important element that
is not available for the majority of the women in this country.
8.1 Current Transportation and Safety Problems
The intensity of transportation and safety concerns varied across participants’ situations. In a few
cases, it is the lack of safe transportation facilities during long routes or after hours for women. For
example, suburban university students shared about the complexity of traveling to the capital city
of Dhaka to participate in national-level events relating to programming, learning, and sharing as
P26 from Rajshahi shares:
Also one major issue I face is that, in my daily life I’ve classes from day to afternoon. I
love to do problem solving which we say competitive programming here, more specif-
ically we have a separate lab open 24/7 to do practice. But being female, I can’t stay
my evening or time during 7pm - 10pm in the lab due to the safety issue I may have
to face while returning home. Being female I have to make sacrifices the night time
practice at the lab cause I’d face safety issue and the males won’t have to face.
The lack of safety significantly impacts the opportunities to learn and grow for female partici-
pants as P8 shared in her letter to M3s: In our country there are some safety issues for women. I think
this is the main barrier for the women and that’s why family dosen’t want to their child go outside
to work. The safety challenge was not only a concern for inter-city travels, it impacted the regular
practices in the capital city. A participant S13, currently pursuing higher studies shared how she
was never able to complete the programming contests which started after their classes and took
a while to finish up which she eventually dropped as: I never finished the entire programming
contest, at the end I stopped participating. The lack of safe transportation facility and the overall
lack of safety in the country impacted the growth and activities of women in computing directly
and indirectly.
The problem with transportation and safety continues from student life till the professional
journey. It is often the lack of transportation that is the problem. A student participant P23, in her

letter to M3, shared the difficulties: Again, the transportation system in Bangladesh is not suitable
for women. Often cases are seen in public transport. In peak time, it is very difficult for women to have
ride in bus. The situation does not get easier for professionals, as a software engineer participant
S6 shared,
We have no transportation system right now. I don’t get CNG or rickshaw. I am afraid
of bikes but I had to use them because I have no other option. Sometimes you have to
make choices to make things work. After working whole day this transportation is a
big hassle.
Parents as participants shared about harassment and safety concerns they fear and have expe-
rienced. A mother as participant, S17 shared about changing their neighborhood for the safety
concerns: We used to live in Bonosri where boys would make comments about my daughter, now we
moved here. The situation is getting worse day by day. Another parent participant P16, shared how
her daughter was irritated from her roadside street harassment:
My daughter was telling me, when she was walking by the street, a stranger (male)
started calling out with “Meow Meaow” sound. She could not ignore it. Later she real-
ized that he made that sound referring to the contact lenses she was wearing. I am so
frustrated with society, can’t our daughters walk in peace?
The safety and transportation related concerns are handled at a personal level with resources
such as a personal transportation system or having a location in one of the secured places in
Bangladesh which is not generic for all the women requiring attention to be paid here.
8.2 Design Approaches to Address Transport and Safety
The professionals considered it as a major challenge and worked on it mainly on a personal basis
rather than seeking support from their organizations, mostly from the fear of being discriminated
against. The student participants were hopeful and wished for changes that did not exist in the
current format.
The student participants meticulously proposed solution approaches to address the safety and
transportation challenges together - mostly looking at ways to introduce safe transportation ser-
vices during the design sessions.
The solutions had different categories; some asked for female-only transportation services while
others wanted to integrate safety mechanisms using connections to law-enforcement agencies.
Few ambitious ideas used artificial intelligence to detect abuse or harassment in the vehicle, a
situation that is not uncommon.
A realistic solution to ensure female seats in current public transports were suggested along
with female drivers by P37 during design session as: Any time transportation service. Available
seat for females in any transport. Available transport in rural areas. Female Uber or Pathao driver.
There was a simple assertion of asking for a female driven vehicle like P20 asked: Dedicated female
transportation service. Some participants, like P33 did not constrain her thoughts seeking a detailed
design as follows:
Increase surveillance in public transport. Track the transport as the transport will be
registered in government application. Application will be featured with transport loca-
tion. CC camera, emergency button, location tracker in the public buses. After pressing
the emergency button it sends the signal to the central through the tracker and sends
the notification to the nearest station.

Fig. 8. (a) Application design to ensure safety. (b)Safe vehicle. (c) Female driver perceived by participants.
Fig. 9. Participants wish for safe navigation.
The solutions provided insights of student participants. Figure 8(a) shows an application devel-
oped to ensure safety. The illustrations in Figure 8(b) show several elements - mostly applicable for
long distance travels - the presence of well-lit roads with surveillance, an in-vehicle surveillance
with the female drier deriving the vehicle and road-side washrooms for women that has sanitary
products. It also shows the lack of support system for women during inter-city travels. The third
solution in Figure 8(c) shows ways of engaging female drivers where they are allowed to make
mistakes. The solutions ask for a safe environment and secured transportation.
Some of the student participants engaged in design discussions showing their desired world
where they are able to navigate it safely as can be seen in Figure 9. It shows the simple desire to
access the roads at nights, the playground or a concert without being questioned, judged, or abused.
These challenges are generic for women rather than specifying women in computing. However, the
open support for any woman is desired and it allows larger opportunities for women in computing
as the study has shown.
The design discussions around transportation and safety showed how it impacted the
participants.

9 Discussion
Women in computing, in the context of Bangladesh, are considered to be ones with greater privi-
leges compared to many other women in this region. These women have completed their higher
secondary exams, and remained in the trail of sciences by the time many female students drop out.
On top of that, computer science and engineering being the popular choice for students, requires
students to avail their spots by competitive entrance exams. We want to explore their positionality
from the empowerment framework.
9.1 Naila Kabeer’s Empowerment Framework
We have considered Naila Kabeer’s framework to analyze the empowerment of women in com-
puting [73]. A framework that has been designed and developed in the context of women living
in Bangladesh initially, later expanded to a broader regional context. This framework looks at the
access to resources, agency towards utilizing the resources, and finally, receiving an achievement
as a result, to analyze the empowerment of women. Our findings are related to empowerment since
the aim of the work is to explore how women in computing succeed beyond tertiary level educa-
tion. The basic requirements of access to resources, agency to make independent decisions and
act on it, and finally to achieve a desirable goal, relates to the exploration on needed elements
to succeed. The elements defined by participants shows how gendered structures have hampered
resource access such as acquiring adequate skills and knowledge in the field of computing; the
agency required by one to make sure one can pursue their professional lives or even choose the
subject of their choice (e.g., computing) beyond gendered expectations; and finally, to be able to
achieve and to continue with a professional journey.
In this discussion, we consider the gender lenses to follow the journey of women in computing
from tertiary level education to professional pathways, to understand their access to resource,
agency and achievements, which are evident from our study as shown in Figure 10. The figure
shows how the findings relate to the elements required in the empowerment framework along with
the existing barriers as explored from this study. It is evident from Figure 10 that access to resources
is the first requirements for a woman to succeed from the framework. Here, the access elements
are contextualized for women in computing. Empowerment then requires agency which is often
hampered in many ways and requires great support to ensure one is able to act independently

which relates to our study requirements towards success. Finally, the path towards achievement
that allows empowerment relates to the success of women in computing as presented through the
framework. There are individual privileges and barriers of the participants of our considerations
and the participant pool is not generalizable. However, taking a close look at this participant pool
would enable understanding of the overall challenges and opportunities women face.
The rest of the subsections explore the empowerment framework elements relating to the study
exploration.
9.2 Resource
Our study confirms the existence of access barriers for women in computing, similar to the exist-
ing body of research (e.g., [6, 68, 90]). Although the women are expected to have equal access to
resources regardless of their gender, there are existing social and structural barriers for women
and according to the empowerment framework, women should get access to such resources. Some
of the resources are structural resources consisting of academic resources and transportation, and
some resources remain through social norms through certain social values and norms impacting
women.
The study shows personal development, learning support along with a requirement for safety
to be major elements required for success of a woman in computing. Having a majority of the
participants to be female computer engineering students, it is expected that the students would
receive the learning support and additional support without gender based barriers. From a high
level overview, the access to resources, particularly academic and learning related ones, appear
to be uniform. Among the structural resources at the academic institutes- the learning facilities,
the laboratories, and residential halls appear to be equally accessible to students once a student is
enrolled. However, a deeper exploration shows the implicit barriers towards women. The barriers
are similar to other studies in the same region or in the South Asian region showing barriers
women face. There is uneven access to lab equipment in laboratory-based learning, unequal access
to labs, group study opportunities for students residing in residential halls where the evening rule
restricts female students to return to their residence by sunset and the rule does not apply to male
students, lack of internet access in female residential halls for their secured locations within the
campus, and so on [6, 68, 90]. Moreover, there is social bias against women among lab instructors,
technicians, and faculty members and, most importantly, among family members. Some of these
social biases are validated using religious rules and remain uncontested. It shows limitations on
equitable academic resource access for women in computing in Bangladesh, hampering the skills
they acquire.
The access to resources are not always hampered by structural barriers. In many cases, the
social barriers, often present in subtle ways create challenges for women. There are challenges
that are guided by patriarchal values as the study shows where in-laws, parents, or peers are
providing gendered behavior as the study shows, hampering access to resources which in turn
impacts self-efficacy. Our study shows a faculty or an employee is able to show gender bias without
being questioned about it. The social validation of patriarchal norms continues the access barriers.
Inability to address the access limitations indirectly supports the regional patriarchal norms that
has limited women in the technology space [122, 123]. The existing patriarchal social norms in the
South Asian context, specifically in Bangladesh, use ‘supportive masculinity’ [38]; that restricts
women’s access to resources, justifying it by supporting their wellbeing and safety [108]. The
obedience of social-cultural norms to ensure women’s access to resources, as has been suggested
by contemporary researchers [123], places a potential risk of continuing the suppression with
cultural validation. The social approval to discriminate against female students, colleagues, and
employees by male (and sometimes female) members of society creates long-term access problems.

The lack of safety limits women of all ages, backgrounds, and residences and has limited their
mobility, severely further contributing to the access barrier. This study showed how the lack of an
adequate transportation system with safety concerns constraints women in computing to acquire
additional skills, also impacting learning, exploration, and commuting to workplaces. A country
led by women for more than a decade [39, 78], referring to priorities of female education and
empowerment [114], has not been able to secure transportation routes for women [118, 132, 133].
There has been rising numbers of incidents of group rape, harassment, and even murder of women
in public transportation [118, 132, 133]; often the incidents are given religious validity in various
informal channels (e.g., social media, communication channels) [98]. The lack of action towards
the abuse and harassment towards women in the public sphere contributes to the problem further.
The lack of safety for women is identified as women’s problems rather than pointing out the lack
of actions to address the concerns which again supports the existing social patriarchal norms.
It is clear from the study and existing literature that adequate access to resources would posi-
tively contribute to women’s skill development and growth.
9.3 Agency
Based on Naila Kabeer’s framework, agency refers to the ability to take action. The ability to access
resources towards empowerment requires the agency allowing independent decision making and
ability to take actions. Our study shows the second ingredient required for success to be a strong
support system and support from professional network and the final ingredient to be having safety.
These requirements are needed for women to take independent actions.
The study shows how the lack of support from families, peers, or mentors can create barriers
that impact one’s confidence level that is needed for independence. The confidence is built up
slowly from childhood and gets affected through lived experiences from families, surroundings,
and society. The lack of support from families, peers, teachers, or mentors from academic or pro-
fessional environments have impacted women’s perception about their abilities and affected their
confidence level, as the study showed. The challenges are sharper when the negligence or lack of
cooperation was justified by religious rules, e.g., male-peers not considering their female classmate
as their group member. The religious justifications remain acceptable by the society and are rarely
questioned about its authenticity. Fighting the rights of women with religious justification remains
a critical problem since suppression is often justified with religious values [75, 136]. Although there
is a growing interest and discussion on design using Muslim Feminism, Islamic HCI concepts, tak-
ing into account the cultural values of Muslim women [88, 89], having the religion based decision
making creates representation challenges since the majority of the religious authorities are held by
men [72]. The influence of religion in violence against women provides a contemporary perspec-
tive to the problem. The recent victimization of a university graduate, Sumaiya, was murdered by
her husband because Sumaiya wished to pursue a career which her husband and in-laws did not
want [16]. She continued to prepare for her career entrance exam, disagreeing with the imposed
barriers on her. She tried to practice her agency against the socially acceptable role. The murder
was publicly supported by many, as presented in Figure 11 in the light of religious justifications.
The comments included “ [...] Why did you get married if you wanted to do whaterver you want.
Keep in mind it is a Muslim Country [...]. Do not create conflict by making contradictory news here”,
“Since the heaven of the wife is under the feet of women, I think women should obey what the hus-
band says. [...]” and “Murder is never justified. However, the girl will stay in Dhaka to become judge
barrister showing her thumbs up to husband’s opinion. [...] “. The murder victim was not a woman
in computing but was a woman from non-urban background who wished to pursue her career after
graduation. The religious justifications towards her murder posted on the online portal of the national
newspaper that was uncontested, not moderated showed its societal acceptance. It is not uncommon to

Fig. 11. Comments justifying the murder of Sumaiya.
see victim blaming at a higher rate towards women pursuing careers and it shows why a strong sup-
port system is essential for women’s empowerment as well as success. These religious justifications
are rarely contested, and thus, these validations remain and continue – many years after women’s
initial liberation towards education.
Exercising women’s agency becomes challenging in the close knit societal structure that is prac-
ticed in Bangladesh [64]. The culture and practice of respecting the elderly and family heads rep-
resent the patriarchal structures where women play subordinate roles. A personal decision of a
woman becomes a concern of a larger community collectively and women struggle to use their
agency in such patriarchal decision making processes [120]. The society defines the adequate age
for a woman to get married; it also defines what is a better subject to study or a better career path to
pursue. For example, the social cultural practices and expectations have determined the priorities
of women to get married at a certain age as this study showed. It impacted students studying at the
tertiary level, many of whom have dropped out during the study period. The participants shared
about losing friends through their study period along with the personal pressure they faced from
families to get married. The agency to pursue one’s own dream was mostly related to the trust and
support families have put up for their daughters. Again, for a younger group of women, the entry
level struggle to pursue computing as a career becomes a problem where women are expected to
obey the family level decisions. A practice of agency to pursue the subject beyond society’s ac-
cepted subject as medicine creates an emotional burden on them. It was easier for those working
women in computing to ensure their agency who had economic independence, giving them better
agency. Again, the agency was required mostly to fight social barriers. The general societal prac-
tices that hamper women in Bangladesh impacts women in computing as well since they are all
part of this close-knit family structure and social practices.
In the presence of all the social challenges, a number of women in computing have pursued
their careers and continued their studies with dreams to pursue a great career in their future. The

participants fighting various barriers and navigating the paths have shared how important the role
of their support system is. Many of these women in computing being in the workforce have been
able to fight some social barriers, some through their unconditional social and network support,
some utilizing their economic independence, and some being away from families abroad to avoid
such barriers. The study clearly shows how a strong support system and existence of role models
can impact women in computing to move forward and practice their agency. It is similar to other
regional studies showing the positive impact a network can create [8].
9.4 Achievement
The study shows women in computing pursue a journey of learning, exploring, and contributing
against many social and cultural barriers towards being an achiever based on the empowerment
framework.
The achievement shows the final element of empowerment based on Naila Kabeer’s framework.
We try to connect achievement to success defined in this study, constituting entry into a job sector
in a relevant field for women in computing. Our study defines the successful persona as one who
has already achieved success despite facing existing barriers. The elements participants shared
that are required for success are not impossible ones and exist in many gender-neutral regions.
The structural barriers are not related to resource constraints but to the systematic practice of
patriarchal rules. The practices can be reduced and entirely removed by designing and practicing
strong gender-sensitive policies [56]. The definition of gender roles through media and other ex-
ploratory forms can play a positive role in presenting the economic stability and success of women
in computing. This can address the ongoing social bias from families, facilities, and institutions.
The safety concern has remained a major constraint in the majority of the research exploring chal-
lenges women in computing consider [108, 109, 120]. It should be a national priority to ensure
transportation and safety for any woman or minority for positive growth as a nation.
The global scenario for successful women in computing as achievers is filled with broader
perceptions paired with local ones [56]. The parameters for success would require us to address
the existing barriers collectively to ensure one is able to pursue one’s dreams without societal
boundaries. The problems affecting women in computing in Bangladesh are a loss for the entire
global community and thus require a collective effort to highlight, encourage, and inspire women
in computing across borders.
The elements needed for women to succeed, relating to the empowerment framework of Naila
Kabeer, apply to women in general beyond women in computing. This direction can be considered
for researchers interested in supporting women or marginal ones in a different context.
10 Limitations
The research work did not include the policymakers as stakeholders which requires involvement
beyond the academic structure. We hope to engage the policy-level stakeholders and connect them
to the learners and other stakeholders to ensure a positive dialogue towards possible future policy
interventions.
11 Conclusion and Way Forward
In this research, we have taken the ambitious approach to explore the necessary elements for women
in computing to succeed, considering the existing constraints in Bangladesh. The study initiates
with exploring the existing body of literature mainly focusing on challenges women in computing
face and to complement the exploration in solution space, it engages a total N=71, (48 tertiary
level female students and 23 stakeholders) in the research. The student researchers engage in
communication with two fictional characters through the Fictional Inquiry (FI) workshops and

then works on designing solution approaches using Co-Design process taking place in Dhaka,
Sylhet, Rajshahi, and Chottogram. The first two workshops were on understanding the barriers
along with their intensity using a fictional prompt. In the first workshop, we used the fictional
prompt of a kind woman named Oporajita, eager to understand the annoying challenges of the
participants. The participants received individual letters from Oporajita, and during the workshop,
all responded to it individually, all remaining in a shared working space which ended in a group
discussion of sharing their thoughts with researchers. The second workshop worked in the same
way, except for the fact that the participants here received a letter from a male fictional character,
M3, who questioned women’s ability (the details of the fictional prompt selection and design
process is present in the Methodology section). The third workshop allows the participants to
reflect on their previous responses, followed by individual design solution propositions, working
in the shared space. It followed a group reflection. The structural and social barriers that came
from a series of workshops allowed us to design queries for stakeholders who shared their views
and pathways for women in computing. We have designed multiple personas of successful women
in computing as a process prior to finalizing the elements for success. The study finalizes three
major elements for women in computing to succeed professionally: 1. provision to improve skills
and self-efficacy, 2. ensuring ways to increase the sense of belonging, and 3. providing transporta-
tion and safety. These elements are analyzed through Kabeer’s empowerment framework [73].
The elements of success show that there is a collective responsibility from families, educational
institutes, and authorities to ensure a safe learning environment, allowing space for growth,
free from societal biases, restrictions, and expectations. This research thus calls for a collective
solution from the larger body to support women in computing beyond regional boundaries.
The work presented from the perspective of women in computing applies to women or mar-
ginal communities in other contextual layouts. The learning barriers would be similar for women
or socially marginal communities when pursuing a topic not traditionally pursued by women or
the marginal community of interest. Similarly, the empowerment framework defined pathways
towards achievement or success relating to women or other marginal communities working un-
der similar social prejudices. The lessons learned are expected to generate conversations around
neutral learning environments, collective support systems, and enhanced safety in the future.

Meena Needs a Computer Now: Co-design Solutions to
Barriers Using Fictional Inquiry for Women in Computing
NOVA AHMED, ECE, North South University, Dhaka, Bangladesh
TASMIAH TAHSIN MAYEESHA, Information Science, University of North Texas, Denton,
Texas, USA
IFTI AZAD ABEER, SUMIT KUMAR KAR, ANIK SAHA, ANIK SINHA, SUMAYA AKTER
RUHI, and MD. HUSSAIN SHAHRIAR, DIAL, ECE, North South University, Dhaka, Bangladesh
SUMAYA YASMIN and NAZMUN NAHAR, ECE, North South University, Dhaka, Bangladesh
SYEDA SHABNAM KHAN, DIAL, ECE, North South University, Dhaka, Bangladesh and ECE, RMIT,
Melbourne, Australia
Gender disparity in computing is a well-explored concern. To complement existing research, we use a non-
intrusive exploration method of Fictional Inquiry. Followed by co-design workshop to explore solution
approaches to increase women’s participation in computing. The study involved n = 48 Women in Computing
(WiC) students in computing from four universities across Bangladesh. Participants shared their challenges
and desired solutions which we analyzed using qualitative methods along with Natural Language Processing
based tools to illustrate the problems from various perspectives while minimizing potential biases. The research
team reflects on methodological decisions, policy implications, and the need for culturally and contextually
appropriate tools and datasets to better support WiC research in resource-limited settings.
CCS Concepts: • Human-centered computing → Empirical studies in HCI;
Additional Key Words and Phrases: Women in Computing, stereotype barriers, ICTD, Qualitative-NLP
analysis
