Needs a Computer Now: Co-design Solutions to Barriers Using Fictional Inquiry for Women in Computing.
ACM Trans. Comput.-Hum. Interact. 33, 1, Article 13 (February 2026), 51 pages.
https://doi.org/10.1145/3762808
1 Introduction
The title of this article refers to Meena, a female cartoon character designed to break gender
stereotypes in South Asia. In the early 2000s, Meena’s stories raised awareness about the importance
of girls’ education. Many young girls inspired by Meena are now female students in computing
at the tertiary level in 2023. They are now considering effective ways to address societal barriers
to pave their pathway for Women in Computing (WiC). The societal barriers resulting in
underrepresentation of WiC is a long-standing problem worldwide and has been explored in
numerous prior works [23, 24, 56–58, 61]. According to Clark, there may be a “leaky pipeline” of
women as they drop out at various phases of tertiary education toward final career goals [56].
Despite various initiatives by the government and companies to achieve gender parity in computing,
the representation of women remains low even in developed regions [31, 58, 61]. It is present in
economically stable countries or countries that have addressed gender neutrality very seriously.
For example, the number of WiC has been steadily declining over the years in USA over past
few decades [94, 95], and the number is low in a gender-neutral country like Norway [96]. This
problem is more acute for the marginalized women in South Asia who face significantly larger
barriers such as sociocultural norms, influences, and infrastructural issues because of limited
resources [24, 25, 51]. WiC research in Asia has focused on the socio-cultural context primarily
exploring the challenges women face while entering a computing career showing strong regional
and cultural influence [23–25, 29–33]. These research brought forth the existing challenges and
various practices to address them to increase WiC representation [23, 24, 29–33, 56–58, 61, 94–98].
This work complements existing research by exploring how WiC perceive barriers when expressing
themselves freely through letter writing, without fear of judgment. It examines the intensity of
their feelings and provides design options to address these barriers. Using innovative methods and
analysis, this research investigates the desired solutions and the intensity of perceived barriers
among tertiary-level computing students in a developing country.
Research works in Bangladesh have revolved around policy and infrastructural suggestions
provided by the researchers [3–7, 10]; however, participant-centered solution design approaches are
not explored with similar rigor and leave space for exploration. While many of the challenges has
been mentioned in prior work, understanding the intensity of barriers faced by WiC in Bangladesh
is important. For instance, Iftekhar et al. highlight peer prejudice faced by women in labs, labeling
women as “less competent” [10]. However, studies from other Global South regions, such as India
and Namibia [23, 97, 98], do not report similar prejudices. The impact of such biased comments
on female peers in Bangladesh remains unexplored. While previous research indicates structural
exclusion from advanced training and evening lab access, the students’ perspectives on the intensity
of this exclusion are missing [3–7]. Given the exclusionary gendered experiences from close and
respected individuals like family and faculty, an indirect method was necessary to capture these
experiences. To understand the subtle social barriers women face, we framed our exploration
in context by asking participants through Fictional Inquiry (FI) methods [18]. We wanted
the participants to bypass existing socio-cultural norms or structures by prompting them with
partially fictional artifacts or scenarios used in FI providing the participants a non-intrusive space

to express themselves. By doing FI, we found strong emotional responses toward authoritative
figures such as teachers and parents, and infrastructural issues of educational institutions. To enrich
our analysis, we used in-depth analysis of the FI responses using qualitative methods as well as
Natural Language Processing (NLP)-based analysis to visually understand the overall scenario.
NLP has significantly advanced qualitative research across various domains [80–85]. Sentiment
and emotion mining, specific NLP techniques, uncover underlying intentions and opinions in data.
Traditional text analysis interprets content, while sentiment analysis reveals emotional subtext. In
our study, we used NLP models to analyze participants’ quotes from letters, alongside a codebook
annotated by qualitative researchers for detailed analysis and visualization. This approach clarified
the emotional expressions and sentiments in the letters. After identifying perceived barriers through
FI, we co-designed solutions with female computing students, incorporating their voices [1]. This
process allowed participants to envision solutions beyond existing limitations, highlighting the
priorities and challenges of WiC.
We involved 48 female undergraduate participants from computer science and engineering
disciplines across Dhaka, Rajshahi, Sylhet, and Chattogram divisions. Each region’s participants
engaged in two FI workshops, sharing challenges through letters to different personas, followed by
a co-design workshop to develop solutions. While FI-based methods and co-designing solutions
have been used in education [19], they have not been applied to address WiC issues. Partici-
pants proposed various solutions, including policy and technical interventions to enhance the
learning environment, increase family and societal support, and improve transportation facil-
ities. This research incorporates the voices of female undergraduate students, presenting their
ideas to the Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) community without making specific design
recommendations.
While existing literature includes qualitative studies on WiC in Bangladesh, our novel use of FI
employs indirection and non-verbal communication to elicit responses participants might fear to
express publicly due to social prejudices. Using NLP-based exploratory visualizations, we uncover
hidden sentiments of fear and sadness from FI workshop letters. Our work brings together FI and
NLP in a context where such interdisciplinary combinations remain rare, particularly in studies
on marginalized WiC in the Global South which opens new possibilities for investigating socially
taboo topics among marginalized communities. Rather than applying NLP models blindly, we
adopted a cautious, context-sensitive approach grounded in qualitative insights. Aware that most
pretrained models are developed using datasets that underrepresent Global South contexts, we
treated their predictions as one signal within a broader analytic process. Our workflow began
with manual review of participant language to identify recurring patterns, linguistic markers,
and cultural references. We then used existing sentiment and emotion classification models to
analyze the data but interpreted the outputs through a comparative lens—crosschecking them
against human annotations informed by domain expertise. This allowed us to identify systematic
misclassifications, particularly where models struggled with sarcasm, mixed emotions, or cultural
nuance. We integrated qualitative validation and domain-aware evaluation to show how NLP tools
can be applied responsibly in underrepresented contexts, while exposing their limitations and
potential failure modes.
As we have applied FI in the context of WiC in Bangladesh, our study adds to the growing body of
regionally grounded design research in HCI and Information and communication Technology
for Development (ICTD). It surfaces participant-defined priorities and structural critiques and
shows how tertiary students are influenced in their academics by teachers, parents, and peers,
complementing existing studies by illustrating the intensity of their problems and giving voice to
their ideas. The research underscores the need for continued efforts to support WiC in South Asia,
ensuring that any girl can aspire to this field without prejudice.

This article contributes to the HCI community in following key ways:
—First, we adapted FI to the context of WiC in Bangladesh, where it remains underexplored.
While FI has been used in education and HCI for discussing sensitive issues [19, 101], our
use focuses on gendered constraints in computing education, providing a new application in
this cultural and disciplinary context. We aimed to help participants to express their feelings
non-verbally, under the disguise of communicating with fictional personas while writing
letters to imaginary characters designed from the societal and historical elements presented
in the related context.
—Second, this work presents a user-defined, solution-focused approach using co-design work-
shops to address societal, structural, and resource-related challenges faced by WiC. Female
tertiary-level students proposed tangible interventions—through policy suggestions, through
drawings, app layouts, and flowcharts, to improve conditions for women in computer science.
This contrasts with traditional approaches where researchers recommend solutions on behalf
of participants.
—Third, we used NLP models to explore the data visually, such as sentiment and emotion
analysis to examine the emotional tone of the letters and workshop discussions. While general
models have limitations when applied to culturally situated texts, they helped us identify broad
emotional trends. These visualizations supported our qualitative coding and interpretation,
allowing us to explore the emotional depth of responses expressed through both language
and non-verbal forms.
—Finally, we present our methodological reflections and lessons learned, shaped by our reflexive
analysis of our own positionalities as NLP and HCI researchers. These include practical insights
on using NLP tools with cultural sensitivity, recognizing model biases, and exploring FI as a
participatory method for imagining more inclusive policies. These reflections are especially
relevant for feminist and cross-cultural HCI and NLP research.
2 Background: Tertiary Education Landscape of Bangladesh
In our work, we focus mainly on the context of Bangladesh, a densely populated country of 173
million people that have almost equal gender distribution [42].
2.1 Challenges in Generic Technology Access and Exposure
Socially there is practice of patrilineal descent (influence of patriarchy), and patrilocal residence
(where women move to live with their husbands and relatives) [43]. Studies have shown how social
norms and religious beliefs limit women’s familiarity and use of technology [41]. Apart from social
challenges, there are infrastructure barriers, for example, in rural areas, Internet connection is
poor, paired with travel restrictions hampering access to publicly available internet access points
like tele centers or Internet cafes. In addition, sometimes, there are restrictions on women on use
of personal mobile phone [100]. The lack of exposure, unequal distribution of household chores,
and their lack of confidence in their capacity for science and technology contribute to the gender-
based digital divide [37]. Women are often more vulnerable to technology-mediated abuse such as
cyberstalking, impersonation, and personal content leakage as a result of this [11, 13, 14, 55]. In
addition, women are expected to behave in certain ways online and as a result many hide their
identities or sentiments [9, 11, 12, 14]. Students’ educational experiences are also harmed by these
infrastructure problems [15, 17]. However, our work here focuses on WiC, where they are assumed
to have the capability to navigate the technology space more fluently.

2.2 Women in STEM and ICT Education
According to Global Gender Gap Report 2023, Bangladesh ranks first in South Asia in terms of
gender parity and 59th globally; however the educational attainment subindex reveals a persistent
gap in enrolment in tertiary education [46]. The country has a high dropout rate in the transition
from higher secondary to tertiary-level education as around 22.72% of students drop out after
higher secondary education.
At the tertiary level, there are 164 universities offering tertiary education in Bangladesh; however,
female representation is low as only 37.58% of total students and 29.79% of total teachers are women.
There is a limitation of data as enrollment of computing specifically was not addressed in Bangladesh
Education Statistics 2022 [47]. Gender-based socioeconomic and cultural barriers like child marriage,
early motherhood, and violence against women are key factors in women dropping out of higher
education [40, 53].
Recent work has suggested although women students’ enrolment at the tertiary level has in-
creased over the years, their representation in STEM fields remains low for multiple reasons includ-
ing societal perceptions, poor infrastructure, and prejudice [44, 49]. The Government of Bangladesh
has introduced gender-sensitive policies to increase female enrolment which is achieved in Primary
and Secondary education levels [44, 45]. The country has ICT education mandatory from grade 6 to
12, but these programs have not focused on computing education in tertiary level [44, 48]. “Digital
Bangladesh,” an initiative to promote ICT accessibility in all areas of Bangladesh, was introduced
in 2008 [54], but these are generic initiatives not focused on computing students.
The first formal computer science program in Bangladesh was introduced in 1982 in BUET [50].
Currently, there are many institutes in Bangladesh that offer computer science and engineering
degrees; however, only few of them are accredited by Board of Accreditation for Engineering and
Technical Education (BAETE) [51]. Previous work showed that enrolment in CS majors, continuation
of study, involvement in competitive programming, and future plans are highly impacted by the
mindset, economic, and sociocultural position of the belonging family [7].
3 Related Work
Exploring the status of WiC in the Asian region in comparison to Bangladesh will help us to
contextualize the current problems.
3.1 Status of WiC in Asia
For underrepresented regions, the literature often focuses on general ICT access and training,
instead of women in tertiary education in computing. It was found that “the notion of a gender
divide in how men and women relate to computing, traditionally attributed to gender differences, is
largely a result of cultural and environmental conditions. Indeed, the reasons for women entering—or
not entering—the field of CS have little to do with gender and a lot to do with environment and culture
as well as the perception of the field” [23]. In many South Asian regions Women’s education is often
viewed as unimportant, and families under-invest in women’s education [28].
Among Asian countries, there is significant diversity in the participation and engagement of
WiC depending on the country and the culture. Being attracted to the stability and the well-paid
jobs in engineering and medicine, many parents push their students to enroll in computing for CS
and IT jobs in India [24, 26, 27]. However, the safer IT offices are not safe since there are security
concerns when women travel and for work shifts that are late at night or late because of physical
safety issues [24, 25]. Parents often create pressure of marriage to female students as a solution to
social problems [24].

However, not all countries are fortunate enough to have a strong representation of women in
the ICT field. Research on Nepal shows that issues like a lack of gender-sensitive ICT policies, high
female poverty, and the perception that ICT careers are more suited to men hurt the engagement of
women [35]. A study on technology access and usage among women of Afghanistan mentioned that
while the women have strong familiarity with technology, they face challenges like inadequate ICT
laws for handling online abuse, social restrictions on visiting public internet cafes [36]. Bangladeshi
women also face many similar challenges.
Another perspective is, however, seen in many Muslim countries like Malaysia, Kuwait, and Saudi
Arabia which show high representation of WiC and have markedly different gender perceptions
around having a career in computing. Computer science is not seen as a masculine or feminine
field, and the perspective is gender-neutral in these cultures [29, 30, 32, 33]. Families encourage
women to enroll in computing for diverse reasons, including intrinsic interest, higher income,
government scholarships, and increased job opportunities [29, 30, 32, 33]. Particularly fathers
often encourage their daughters to enroll in computing for financial and security reasons and
indoor office job opportunities [29, 30]. A culturally positive perception of WiC, optimistic attitude,
female role models, as well as government policies on the education of women with a focus on
ICT and quota systems helped Malaysian women to make strides in computing [29–31]. Although
some gendering was seen even in favored conditions, such as physical activities like working with
electronics, networking, and civil engineering majors where fieldwork is involved were looked
upon as “masculine,” in contrast to software engineering and programming which are considered
theoretical and fit for women [29, 30]. In some Muslim countries, faculties can be both female
and male, but in classroom settings, female-only gender-segregated classrooms are used [32, 34].
Our study, in contrast, involved mixed-gender classrooms at the tertiary level and a similar work
environment having participation of all genders. The solutions suggested by participants considered
such environment over gender-segregated classrooms in our findings.
3.2 WiC in Bangladesh
Research on WiC in Bangladesh shows challenges women face including consistent underrepre-
sentation of women in STEM education and related jobs, lack of mentors along with the scarcity of
female role models, unsupportive and exclusionary behavior from male peers, challenges related
to security, transportation, and accessibility-related issues which become obstacle to a career in
computing [3–7, 10, 15–17]. According to a survey of ICT industry in 2018, only 16% of the total ICT
workforce were women [52]. Table 1 shows major work exploration from challenges and proposed
solution perspectives from major works focusing of women that includes study on WiC. These
studies use methods such as surveys interviews, fictional enquiry, focus group discussions, and
various interactions to engage with researchers to identify challenges. The challenges explored
consist of societal ones as well as infrastructural ones that limited WiC in various ways as presented
in Table 1. Finally, the possible solution approaches cover the ranges of ideas suggested or practiced
by the researchers. Our work, on the other hand, tries to focus on barriers in ways without directly
communicating to WiC where they share their current challenges through letter writing and the
possible solution approaches are again suggested by the same group of participants through design
workshops varying from existing work methodologically focusing on the same problem space.
4 Methods
In this research work, we have used two workshops using FI to explore the existing challenges
WiC face. This was followed by a co-design workshop to develop the possible solutions for the
barriers by the same group of participants. We present the details and rationale of these techniques
in the following subsections.

4.1 FI and Co-design
FI to Explore Challenges. In this work, we use FI where participants are able to bypass existing social
challenges as according to Dindler and Iversen, “The central idea of FI is to temporarily change or
bypass existing socio-cultural structures in a given practice … FI allows designers to confront users with
their own practice” [18]. FI uses simple “props” to create partially fictional scenarios and artifacts
to let the participants explore the world through a fictional lens which assists in coordinating or
prompting the imaginings of the participants [18, 20, 21]. It has been used in various contexts such
as education setting for co-designing with preschoolers [19], reimagining museum experiences
[21], designing city games with marginalized communities [20], and producing smart materials
for future [21]. Existing work in education using FI showed enhanced self-expression, liberation
of fear of self-exposure, and stimulation of creativity [22] of students which we have used as our
inspiration.
FI Props. In our FI workshops, we engage the participants in a conversation to fictional characters
to elicit strong emotional responses with letters as our “props” since a letter allows a personal space
for individuals. We used a format of letter writing where letters arrived to participants from two
different personnel where participants responded individually by writing their own letters to these
personas.

Fictional Characters. These fictional characters were created considering local cultural context of
Bangladesh. The group of researchers worked together through their lived experiences to design
the letters in a collaborative manner. One fictional character named Oporajita represented the
support and mentorship women receive from an imaginary female supportive character, written
with a soft tone seeking their challenges (details are provided below describing FI 1). The second
fictional character, M3, was a male who questions women’s intelligence and ability to work outside
written in a harsh tone showing authoritative position presenting negative mindsets exhibiting
traditional stereotypes in our society. This is designed based on challenges referred to the existing
literature and the first authors’ decade-long experience of working for WiC (details are provided
below describing FI 2).
Testing of FI Letters. The letter was initially tested by one phase of response collection and analysis.
The researchers along with two volunteers who were not involved in the research responded to the
letters. Based on the suggestions of all the responders, the letters were modified.
Rationale. The letters written to fictional characters are expected to create a response without any
existing social obligation one may feel so that the participants could share their thoughts to these
characters without any fear or prejudice of hurting their feelings. The varying personalities were
employed to provide both supportive and negative tones to bring out different emotional responses
from participants. Although there have been regional explorations on barriers women face in the
computing field, this research wanted to reach further using FI since it allows the participants to
brainstorm within the context of an imagined reality [18, 19].
Co-design as a Solution Approach. We wanted to engage the participants actively in designing a
solution that is appropriate in their socio-cultural context taking into account existing constraints
using the co-design method. It is used “to refer to the creativity of designers and people not trained in
design working together in the design development process” [1]. It further considers, “users as expert
of their experiences” [63].
In our work, we wanted to design new solution approaches with our participants considering
the challenges they explored through FI workshops. Combining these two methods, we were able
to get participants to generate solutions grounded in their current environment.
4.2 Participant Recruitment
We used purposive sampling to recruit participants from four different divisions of Bangladesh—
Dhaka, Rajshahi, Chattogram, and Sylhet; by approaching Key Informants (KI), a person known
and trusted by the participants [62]. The researchers reached out the KIs through snowball sampling
[104]. The researchers, KI, and the participants had an introductory session before the workshops
establishing a relationship. The participant information is given in Table 1. The information is
provided without referring to their specific institutes to ensure that their identities are protected,
considering the limited number of female students in Computer Science and Engineering programs.
We shared the purpose and moderation of the study with the KIs and asked them to find female
students studying subjects related to computing at the tertiary level—in all the cases, it was students
studying Computer Science and Engineering. The KI explicitly stated the study purpose to the
participants before the workshops. Students who showed interest after having all the information
on the study participated in the workshop. Researchers consulted the KI to select the study location.
The participants from every region participated in three consecutive workshops named Oporajita,
M3, and Co-design of solutions, as presented in Table 2. The participants were recruited for three
consecutive workshops ranging from second year to final year in undergraduate studies except for
Dhaka. In the first study taking place at Dhaka, it was clear that the first year students were not
exposed to all the type of classes (e.g., lab and theory).

4.3 Workshops
There were three workshops—FI 1 Workshop and FI 2 Workshop—to illustrate challenges through
responses from two fictional characters Oporajita and M3 that has a positive tone and a negative
tone, respectively, followed by CD: Co-design Workshop 3 focusing on the solution aspect (the
letters are provided in Appendix A, Figures A1 and A2). Each workshop was conducted on separate
timeframes with the same participants; the time distribution is presented in Table 3. Workshop are
explained in detail later. The FI 1, FI 2, and CD workshop took place in consecutive order starting
with a positive tone, then through a negative one, and finally on a separate day brainstorming
on possible design approaches. The workshops all took place in separate days except for the ones
in Sylhet where the researchers conducted two FI workshop in the same day and realized that
it was tiring process and ensured separate days for each workshop. Each of the workshops ran
once in each region with all the participants where the individual workshop details are given in
the following subsection. A pictorial presentation of the workshops is presented in Appendix B,
Figures B1 and B2.
FI 1: Responding to a Letter from Oporajita, a Fictional Female Character. This letter was from an
imaginary person named Oporajita, a female descendant of Begum Rokeya. Begum Rokeya is a

prominent writer, educator, and thinker who contributed toward the empowerment of Bengali
Muslim women and known as a significant female role model for Bengali women [66].
Oporajita, the female persona shared a bit of Begum Rokeya’s struggle in the past and told the
participants she wishes to continue Rokeya’s will to empower women in Bangladesh. She candidly
asked about how women today are doing as she is hopeful that women have progressed a lot
over all these years. We expected the candidates to hold knowledge about Rokeya as even in our
primary education curriculum her stories are included and framed Oporajita as a descendant of
her lineage to establish a connection of trust and respect. The letter was written in a supportive
tone. The goal of this letter is to explore the current barriers female students are facing where
they can respond to an imaginary supportive role model who envisions women’s freedom through
knowledge acquisition. The letter is attached in the Appendix section. The workshop participants
were asked to read the letter and responded to the letter individually in a written format without
any given word limit or page limit. It was followed by a sharing session where all participants from
the same region joined. The discussion was moderated by a researcher to ensure the presence of
all the voices. The workshop provided necessary stationaries and supplies for the participants to
respond and brainstorm, including papers, pens, pencils, whiteboards, poster boards, color pencils,
markers, and so on.
Workshop 2: Responding to a Letter to Mustakim Muhammad Monsur (M3), a Fictional Male
Character. This letter was from a male imaginary person M3 who holds a position of influence to
make changes for working women. However, in his letter, he is skeptical about women’s ability
and desire to join the workforce. He refers to many of his own female family members who are
more interested in other things rather than pursuing a career. The letter is written in a harsh tone
with judgment. The goal of this letter is to understand the challenges women face after negative
emotional feedback is given. As discussed, in the existing literature, it was found that women in
Bangladesh face discriminatory behavior from male authority figures and peers in both education
and work life. We asked the participants to respond in their letters without any fear, as in real life
they may not have the courage to argue against such people. Similar to FI 1, there was no word
limit to respond to this letter. The letter to M3 is attached in the Appendix section. The supplies
were similar to ones provided in FI 1.
CD: Co-design of Solutions. The co-design workshop oriented around the problems discussed in
the previous workshops. Pre-workshop analysis was done on the responses of the participants in
Workshop 1 and Workshop 2 to identify the key challenges mentioned. These challenges served as a
starting point as we presented them in a presentation slide to the participants. Then, the participants
focused on designing ways to address solutions given as an open-ended problem through co-design,
a technique used as a response in other regions such as Namibia [98]. We allowed space and time
to think about solution approaches toward challenges and provided the participants with a floor to
have an open discussion among themselves. Many participants preferred technology solutions,
being technology students. It was a full day workshop. This workshop was conducted in spaces
agreed upon with the participants that had working space for design and brainstorming. The design
session used the co-design approach where the participants engaged with researchers to work on
solutions. It reflects on an active solution approach since there is a gap in having engagements
coming from participants being WiC.
Since the participants were undergraduate students familiar with general software design and
visualization techniques taught to them in prior courses, many of them preferred creating solutions
around their expertise—designing algorithms, flowcharts, visualizations, and diagrams with stick
figures during the sessions. Some of the participants initiated their design from their imagination
of ways existing barriers can be eradicated where some worked on policy-level changes while

4.4 Qualitative Content Analysis
We have conducted a few rounds of content analysis—initiating with transcribing the audio recorded
during the workshops and coding the initial contents consisting of letters and discussions. The
audio recordings of the discussions during and after FI workshops and the discussions during the
co-design workshops (accumulating to 5.45 hours of audio) were transcribed. After the initial coding
process, we categorized the codes and refined them through several iterations. To identify the key
themes, we used reflexive thematic analysis process [65]. The qualitative researchers engaged in
conducing the workshops worked collaboratively toward data analysis.
The analysis evolved into major initial codes as academic, teacher, advertisement, awareness,
bias, exposure, family, forum, infrastructure, mentorship, networking, security, special situation,
transportation, security, and underrepresentation (presented in Figure 1, right). We present the
regional and overall frequencies of the codes in Table 4. The content from the problem side came
mostly from the letters written to Oporajita and M3 in FI 1 and FI 2 FI workshops, respectively.
The solution-related discussion mainly came from the CD design workshop, some of it was also
suggested in the letters of FI workshops.
For individual themes, we contrasted the challenges along with the solutions and cross aligned
them with the participants’ information, their regions and how the concept emerged through a
letter to Oporajita, to M3, or during the design session. We created individual persona (as presented
in Figure 1, left) and regional persona (as presented in Figure 1, middle) to reflect findings from
challenges and solutions space from that particular region. We further analyzed the data to show the
time references of the topic whether it refers to the levels of primary schooling, middle school, high
school, tertiary level, professional level, and so on. Through the analysis process, the participants’
concepts were considered through various aspects such as individually, according to their study
locations, based on their original residences, and based on other personal interests to thrive, and so
on. We also took into account the observations and personal notes researchers took during the
study process.
For this particular study, we focused mostly on the solutions suggested by the participants
and worked through the solution space suggested by participants. Then, multiple themes were

4.5 NLP-based Analysis
Traditionally, qualitative research involves manually coding interview transcripts, user observation
notes, and survey responses; however, NLP can be a powerful tool to enrich qualitative research by
offering new ways to analyze and understand user data [80–85]. NLP techniques like sentiment
analysis, emotion mining, and named entity recognition can augment the qualitative research.
While NLP models are not perfect, and their accuracy can vary depending on the quality and size
of the training data and researchers need to be aware of potential biases and errors in the NLP
outputs and conduct human review to ensure the validity of the findings, we can identify recurring
themes, participant frustrations, and positive or negative experiences within the data. Previous
work suggests mixed methods research, drawing from both NLP and HCI can allow us to develop
richer and holistic understanding of the narratives given by participants in qualitative research to
analyze larger patterns across stories [67].
Transfer learning is an approach in NLP which saves time and resources by starting with a
pre-trained model that already has learned valuable features about language. Training a sentiment
analysis model from scratch requires a large amount of labeled data which can be expensive and
time-consuming to collect and annotate. Transfer learning allows us to leverage pre-trained models

Our dataset constructed from interview transcripts is small, so instead of training models from

emotion analysis as shown in Figure 2 involves collecting participant responses via conducting
FI and co-design workshops, then annotating the quotes from the letters by grouping them into
codes and themes, preprocessing the data by cleaning and translation, choosing relevant pretrained
models for our analysis, getting the sentiment and emotion scores, and analysis of the outputs via
data visualization techniques. Relevant models along with their data labeling schemas are described
in the following sections.
Annotated Letter Dataset Construction from Participant Responses. To prepare our dataset for
analysis with NLP techniques such as sentiment analysis and emotion mining, after performing
qualitative coding and assigning relevant tags to the interview transcript quotations, we pre-
pared a dataset from our interview transcripts for NLP work. This dataset included following
features—participant ID, participant location, participant quotes from letters sent to M3 and Opo-
rajita in workshop 1 and 2, quotes from design sessions in workshop 3, primary category/code
assigned to the quotes along with sub-categories of challenges and solutions.
Relevant metrics such as number of quotes and tags for this dataset is given in Table 5. The tags
assigned to each quote is the most granular unit of our coding scheme; these were further grouped
into relevant sub-categories and primary categories. Our aim was to clearly differentiate whether
the sentiment and the emotion change when participants express themselves via letters to M3
and Oporajita, two unique individual personas we created for FI workshop. We also additionally
consider the design workshop-related quotations for comparison.
Data Preprocessing. Since the letters were written in both English and Bengali, we used minor
preprocessing before using sentiment analysis and emotion analysis models. We used language
detection tools to detect Bengali along with translation models for translating letter quotes from
Bengali to English. A summary of the tools and models used is given in Table 6.
We selected open source tools from the HuggingFace repository based on accessibility, free in
price, reported performance, and transparency of pretraining data. Here, we document the models
selected for sentiment and emotion analysis.

[70], a RoBERTa-base model trained on approximately 124 million tweets from January 2018
to December 2021 and fine-tuned for sentiment analysis on the TweetEval benchmark [71, 72].
The model incorporates preprocessing steps to reduce potential spam and near duplicate tweets
and employs a continual training procedure. Since the model was originally trained on Twitter

Emotion Analysis Model Selection. For emotion analysis, we used the “j-hartmann Emotion English

analysis [78] and emotion classification of newspaper headlines [79].
Context-aware Sentiment and Emotion Analysis. While we aimed to explore the dataset through
an NLP lens, we remained conscious of the limitations of existing NLP models, particularly the
potential biases embedded in their pretraining datasets due to demographic mismatch and model
assumptions. Thus, prior to applying computational models, we conducted qualitative analysis
of letter quotes to identify emerging trends and patterns in participants’ expressions. We then
applied pre-trained sentiment analysis and emotion classification models to generate prediction
scores for each letter unit (quotes). The computational analysis was structured across multiple
levels of granularity: individual participant responses, regions (location), thematic categories and
sub-categories (specifically examining challenges faced by WiC and their proposed solutions), and
per-letter sentiment and emotional trajectories. The multi-level visualization approach allowed us
to capture both individual experiences and collective patterns in participants’ affective responses
to the gendered personas. This allowed us to explore whether sentiment or emotional tones varied
systematically by theme or participant, and how model predictions aligned, or misaligned, with the
nuances identified in our manual analysis.
Human-centered Model Evaluation with Situated Knowledge. We approached model evaluation
through a reflexive, context-aware lens as shown in Figure 3, that acknowledged our positionalities

as NLP and HCI researchers working across cultural and linguistic boundaries. To ground our anal-
ysis in lived experiences of participants, we manually annotated 20% of the letters using annotators
fluent in local computing discourse, colloquial language, and the gendered sociopolitical context
and compared model output against these human judgments. Our evaluation criteria specifically
examined errors introduced during translation from Bangla to English, instances where model
predictions misaligned with human annotations (including misunderstanding participant intent,
flattening emotional tones, and missing cultural context), and systematic patterns of misrepresenta-
tion. The annotators were computer science students themselves from different backgrounds helped
to surface errors that standard benchmarks often miss, including misclassifications of sarcasm,
erasure of emotional intensity, and cultural mismatches in affect lexicons and systematic patterns
of misrepresentation. We documented them through detailed case studies with direct quotes and
justifications from annotators.
To investigate the source of errors, we also performed a pretraining data audit of the models
used. Since NLP systems are trained on human language, they inevitably inherit social biases, such
as those related to gender or ethnicity, embedded in the pretraining data, which is again a snapshot
of the time (when the data were collected), place (source of data), and assumptions held by the
NLP researchers themselves, as language as inherently situated and shaped by specific cultural
and historical contexts [129, 130]. This perspective informed our use of the Situated Data, Situated
Systems framework [120], through which we used its guiding questions to critically examine how
inherited biases surfaced in our dataset.
4.6 Research Ethics and Incentive
The study is approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) (details redacted for blind review).
On the day of the workshop, we verbally explained the workshop objective, process, and permission
required for recording data and photographs. The participants were adults and verbally agreed and
signed a written consent form. All notes, recordings, photographs, and writings are stored in a
secured drive, which can be accessed by the researchers only.
4.7 Research Team and Positionality
All the researchers in the team were born and brought up in Bangladesh and are familiar with
barriers women face being part of Computer Science and Engineer community. The researchers
are sharing their background and experiences based on Ruth Franeker’s views for readers to
understand the importance of reflexivity in qualitative research [64, 105]. All of the team members
are qualitative researchers with more than 3+ years of research experience and have undergraduate
degrees in computer science from Bangladesh. They have worked on diverse projects spanning
machine learning, HCI research focusing on marginalized communities as well as low-resource NLP.
On the other hand, the quantitative research team for NLP did not have any direct interaction with
participants and worked on the collected dataset from qualitative researchers. All the researchers
are trained with human subject handling as required by the IRB process. The team composition
was balanced in terms of gender, religion, and experience of growing up in urban vs. rural areas.
The team is familiar with the contextual environment of the student participants because they
graduated from local universities and went through similar curriculums, thus they have lived
experience of existing challenges and solutions.
To avoid the social desirability bias [103], the researchers allowed anonymity and complete
confidentiality of the participants in the FI workshops. We used an indirect inquiry method FI
and prepared two different personas for participants to express their viewpoints via letters. It was
further ensured that there was no direct interview process in the study. The research took place
mostly through active participation of tertiary-level students through their writing and design

process which was discussed later with the researchers after an initial introduction. The lack of
direct interaction between researcher and participant during the exploration process minimized
the possibility of social desirability bias. The researchers were friendly and supportive of their
ideas while maintaining neutrality. Faculties were not present during the interviews to avoid the
possibility of the power imbalances with the participants, while the facilitators themselves were
around similar age range (around 3- to 5-year differences).
5 Participant Perception of Challenges and Responses
There were three stages of exploration where participants initially responded by writing letters
to Oporajita who had a supportive tone, followed by another letter to M3 that was negative and
harsh about women’s ability and finally a design workshop that preceded the topics that came
from the letters across participants. In this section, we analyze the perception and attitudes of our
respondents toward the fictional characters presented to them as props from both qualitative and
quantitative perspective. First, we present the qualitative research observations of our respondents
toward two contrasting personas—M3 and Oporajita. Then, we present the results of our sentiment
analysis and emotion mining. The design workshops focused on solutions to existing problems.
The participants discussed the aspects, wrote notes, and diagrams of possible solution approaches
which are presented in the light of problems in the following subsections.
5.1 Qualitative Observation of FI Workshop
The letters had varied levels of emotional engagement of participants even when the participants
were aware of the letters coming from fictional characters being in a respectful interview and
letter writing workshop settings. From our qualitative observations, we found that participants
responded with highly intense emotions for the M3 letters. In the M3 letter, we tried to aggravate
the participants by using language such as women are not as “sharp” as men, lacks “natural talent,”
and not “serious” about computing. Some people found the negative attitude shown by M3 as
personal insults and they used slang, or sarcastic language against the M3 persona to respond. M3
persona was considered as a “real person” by many students where they are clearly calling him by
his name to respond to the letters with sarcastic and harsh reprimands. Some of the participants
used negative words to respond to M3 about this problem calling him “narrow minded,” “low” in
their responses even after knowing it was a fictional character. For example, one of the participants
wrote in her letter the following lines responding to M3:
“First of all, Mr. Mustakim can’t think women are not better than men. He clearly thinks that
women just think about their beauty, shopping bla bla bla, I hope, Mr. Mustakim thinks more
carefully and respectfully about women. Otherwise, it’s his loss … he should not judge all women
with his 3rd class point of views and ideas”—P45.
In contrast to that, Oporajita persona was considered as a supportive female figure by almost all
the participants and the students opened their hearts. Oporajita asked open-ended questions such
as whether the students are still facing “challenges” and “injustices” in the new era. A particular
participant wrote in her letter to Oporajita:
“As a female student, one needs to work a bit harder than the male counterpart to prove their
worth and that’s a bit disheartening in the era of establishing equal rights.”—P36.
The participants described numerous challenges including social injustices from parents and
teachers, infrastructure-related issues, and workplace discrimination. Most of the challenges came
out through the letters where workplace, balancing work and life and career-related concerns were
discussed more in letters to M3, while academic, family, and social concerns came from letters

5.4 Reflection on Power Embedded in Technologies
Justification of Human Evaluation. While we designed our interpersonal interactions to minimize
hierarchical and cultural power imbalances, we recognize that power is equally embedded in
the tools, languages, and infrastructures we used—particularly those related to NLP [120, 129].
Models we employed for text classification rely on pretraining datasets that reflect dominant global
ideologies and linguistic norms, often marginalizing languages like Bangla or underrepresenting
non-Western social contexts [128]. Translation tools, too, are rarely neutral; they prioritize stan-
dardized forms over colloquial, gendered, or context-specific expressions, potentially flattening
the nuances in participants’ voices [132]. Even when models operate without human intervention,
they reproduce systems of exclusion—e.g., by failing to capture the implicit meanings in locally
situated speech, or by prioritizing dataset-defined “accuracy” over cultural relevance [130, 131].
This necessitates ongoing reflection not only on how we interact with participants but also on
the invisible infrastructures that mediate their data. These mismatches risk misinterpreting or
erasing the lived experiences of Bangladeshi WiC. Our team’s own positionalities—as Bangladeshi
researchers with varying degrees of proximity to the tech industry, language fluency, and feminist
ideology—enabled us to recognize many of these misalignments.
5.4.1 Human Evaluation of Model Responses. We have manually annotated 20% of the letter
dataset (both for sentiment and emotions). After annotation, we found that the sentiment model
showed an overall accuracy of 73.26% (positive, 92.86%; neutral, 23.08%; negative, 95.65%) and the
emotion model showed an overall accuracy of 21% for identifying emotions into 7 labels (6 emotions,
1 neutral class). Out of our full dataset, only 8 of the sentences were translated from Bangla. Our
review process included annotators who were familiar with the local context (researchers who
have studied/are studying computer science themselves in their final year of university or who
have already graduated) and who could reflect on local context, sentiment, and slang. This aligns
with the call of Buolamwini and Gebru for algorithmic justice—emphasizing lived experience as a
site of evaluation.
We have documented specific instances where NLP models misrepresented sentiment, tone,
or cultural meaning, accompanied by direct quotes from the data and a clear rationale for why
the output did not align with participants’ intent. These examples will be showcased as case
studies within the article, followed by the participatory review process that allowed annotators
and community members to correct or contextualize the tool’s output. Our evaluation criteria
included errors introduced during translation and mismatches between model prediction and human
annotation (misunderstanding participant intent, flattening emotional tones, missing cultural
context, etc.). A detailed evaluation guideline is given in Appendix E.
5.4.2 Misclassification Analysis of Model Responses. While it is important to critique NLP mod-
els, we must also challenge the automatic assumption that these models are always inaccurate

and consider the relative performance. We initiate our fine-grained analysis beyond accuracy by
analyzing which labels were commonly mislabeled for both sentiment and emotion classification.
According to Figure 9(a), we observe that model predictions for the positive and negative
sentiment labels align well with human annotation (positive 83.33%, negative 75%), while annotators
considered many neutral class predictions as either positive or negative. This signals that the model
failed to pick the nuances of the sentiment in the responses it identified as neutral. In Figure 9(b),
we compare the emotion categories for model responses against human annotation and find that
the most common case of mislabeling was considering sadness as neutral (42%) and joy as neutral
(14%), showing that the model failed to understand the deeper emotional context. Both models
mainly show mistakes in identifying neutral categories. A key reason behind this discrepancy lies
in the differences in annotation targets and model training datasets. Sentiment classification is
inherently coarser, distilled into three broad categories—positive, negative, and neutral—allowing
for more generalizable predictions across datasets. In contrast, emotion detection aims to assign
specific psychological states (e.g., fear, joy, sadness), which are not only more contextually nuanced
but also deeply embedded in cultural, social, and situational cues that general-purpose models often
fail to capture. On top of that even people often disagree in assigning emotional labels [119]. We
expand our analysis with an audit of the pretraining data in the next section.
5.4.3 Pretraining Data Audit of Models. Upon a review of the pretraining and fine-tuning data
sources used for both models, we found that while the sentiment model was trained and fine-tuned
on only Twitter-based conversations [71, 72], mirroring the informal and expressive tone of our
participant quotes, the emotion model was trained on combination datasets like Meld (collection of
dialogues from a popular TV showed called Friends) [75] and GoEmotions (Reddit dataset, western,

young male centric demography) [76] along with Tweets from Twitter [125, 126] and emotion
survey data curated by psychologists [127]. The mismatch of data for emotions may account for
the performance issue, both Meld [75] and GoEmotions [76] contain brief, decontextualized, or
media-centric samples considering western culture more, so these datasets may not reflect the
complex narrative structure and emotional layering of participant letters written in response to
gendered personas. Emotion model may have predicted “neutral” where humans detect “sadness”
because it struggled with contextualization, especially in emotionally ambiguous or indirectly
expressed content. Furthermore, gendered language use and local expressions of vulnerability (e.g.,
expressions of collective struggle or institutional barriers) may not have been captured properly.
5.4.4 Reflecting on Power in Data, Tools, and Knowledge. Inspired by bias-aware “Situated Data,
Situated Systems” frameworks for examining power relations in NLP [120], we conclude with
reflections on four key questions that surface the power dynamics embedded in our methodology:
(1) Who or what is included in the research?
Our study centers first-year women computer science students from four Bangladeshi uni-
versities who wrote personal letters to two personas: M3, a dismissive male figure, and
Oporajita, a supportive female presence. We also include sentiment and emotion analysis
models commonly used in English-language NLP research.
(2) Who or what is excluded?
The models are trained on English-only, Western-centric corpora and emotional taxonomies
(e.g., Ekman’s six emotions), which may not reflect South Asian linguistic and cultural
contexts [121–123]. They also fail to capture the nuance of letters, affective storytelling, or
gendered political expression.
(3) How is knowledge defined?
We treat the letters as situated expressions of emotion and critique—not abstract data. Studies
show that annotator demographics significantly shape sentiment labels, affecting model
performance by over 4.5%. This highlights that what models “understand” as sentiment
reflects whose emotions are centered in training data. Our findings expose how NLP tools
often misalign with the lived realities of our participants, making model validity not just a
technical issue, but a matter of epistemic justice [124].
(4) Who has agency and who is empowered?
Participants exercise partial agency within structural constraints; researchers hold more
power in interpreting, modeling, and framing. While we initially used NLP tools as visual
aids, our error analysis revealed systemic mismatches that called for deeper critique.
Prior work highlights the importance of accounting for annotator demographics when building
and evaluating datasets [124]. The emotion model we used reported 66% accuracy on its original
test set, but this dropped to 21% when applied to our dataset. This stark decline reflects more than
a performance issue—it reveals a demographic and cultural mismatch between the model’s original
annotators and our context. Our Bangladeshi annotators bring situated knowledge shaped by lived
experiences that Western annotators likely do not share. If the same letters had been labeled by a
different demographic, the emotional readings—and thus the model’s “failures”—may have looked
very different. As feminist HCI scholars, we argue that what counts as a failure is not objective;
it is shaped by who is looking, and what assumptions they carry. Tools do not just fail—they fail
someone, and how that failure is named matters. We advocate for context-aware dataset construction
and evaluation along with developing culturally sensitive models that centers participant realities
and community validity—when situating tools in a particular culture such as ours. Even tools like
NLP models must be co-constructed with the communities we aim to serve.

6 Participant-designed Solutions and Recommendations
In this section, we outline the recommendations and solutions designed by the participants in the
co-design workshops we held. The participants designed a variety of solutions for finding support
in their learning environment, family and society, and transportation sector.
6.1 Support in the Learning Environment
Gender-sensitive and -aware teachers, staff, and facilities along with opportunities to collaborate
in groups for further enhancements were discussed through letters written during FI sessions and
solution design sessions by the participants.
6.1.1 Gender-sensitive and -aware Teacher and Staff. The necessity and the impact of gender-
sensitive teachers and staff was an area that clearly came out from the series of workshops. This
topic was not explicitly shared in other studies focusing on WiC in this region [3–7].
Most participants across all the regions strongly referred to the importance and impact of
having gender-sensitive teachers and staff. The topic was intensely discussed in the Rajshahi and
Sylhet region. The solution ideas preceded the points raised through the FI sessions and follow-up
discussions. In the letters written to Oporajita, participants shared faculty members’ negative
attitudes toward female students. The negative mindset came in two forms, one referring to the
attitude that women lack technical ability, and the other one was the lack of necessity for technical
knowledge as women would not be entering the technical job force. One participant strongly shared
her views:
“It would be wrong to say that the gender stereotype in this discipline still lies in my university,
yet it hasn’t completely gone away. I still have teachers in my classroom who underestimate
my ability in lab work. And, on most days I am tired of being labeled as a female engineer, not
just an Engineer.”—P38, Chattogram.
In the design workshops, the solution approaches came where gender sensitivity of faculty and
staff members reappeared through design suggestions. It came in various formats referring to short-
term or long-term exposure of the teachers and staff who have a strong impact on their students.
A participant P20 suggested “gender sensitivity test prior to a faculty hiring process” referring to
the tertiary level, while another participant P15 suggested “counseling on gender sensitivity at the
primary school level.” Another participant boldly shared her desired design process as follows:
“Counseling sessions and mental fitness testing for teachers regarding their mentality problem.
They should treat students equally regardless of gender. [..] Be flexible to students so that they
can communicate without hesitation.”—P25, Sylhet.
The gender-sensitive role requires an active engagement in the entire learning process as partic-
ipants shared. Our participants elaborated on ongoing challenges in congested lab spaces or when
few resources are shared among groups of students during hands-on learning activities. This was
explained by a participant during the design phase:
“In our 1st/2nd semester, we completed some labs based on electrical experiments. We faced
unequal opportunities for advancements or leadership roles during those labs. Most of the
time, all male students successfully did their experiments with the help of the teacher. But we,
females, failed to do our lab as we are a minority group. During those experiments, all male
students made a crowd and completed their experiments as a team. But we are a minority team,
failed to enter that crowd, failed to hear the teacher lecture and so on.”—P43, Chattogram.

The design illustration refers to a psychology test about a teacher’s mental preparedness to teach

If teachers don’t want to communicate with us, it will be tough for us to study there.” The religious

with their female classmates. A participant P47 shared: “Due to religious attitudes or social norms,
many boys do not want to participate properly in class activities with classmates of the opposite sex.
In this case, various group activities or discussions are hindered, and girls lag behind.” The isolation
for strict religious practices was a concern for the learners also; participant P42 shared: “Limited
representation restricts my visibility, voice, and overall influence in these fields.”
The participants directly associated the mindset of teaching and staff members toward the growth
and dreams of female students referring to the very low number of women in tech-industry. The
number of references to gender-sensitive teaching staff in the problem identification phases was
over 24 references by 17 individual participants as well as in the design phase by 13 individual
participants across various regions which shows the importance of this problem.
6.1.2 Facilitation through Wider Exposure and Better Infrastructure. The increased exposure
and learning facility in technology was widely discussed by participants from all the regions.
The topic of better learning facilitation came from two perspectives—prioritizing and facilitating
Information and Communication Technology (ICT) education throughout the country and
focusing on specific infrastructural issues women face. The need for inclusion of ICT at a wider
level with increased rigor was discussed equally through letters to M3 and Oporajita along with the
design sessions. In the second topic discussion, there were considerations about female learners
that were relevant in residential universities outside the capital which came through the design
session.
ICT is given a higher priority at country level where it is included as a subject at high school level
in Bangladesh [8]. Study participants have also emphasized the quality of education and rigor of ICT

learning from younger age as a participant P44 mentions: “Tech competition in higher school level or
basic programming contest at higher school level as ICT subject is introduced at school level.” However,
the students experience ICT knowledge gap for not having enough qualified teachers in this field
as P32 mentions: “To ensure proper teaching of ICT, teachers have to be students of IT background.”
The broader discussion remained about having wider exposure of ICT in major curriculum such
as the National University Curriculum to ensure access of ICT to the root-level students according
to the participant. If more people graduate from ICT, it will open up opportunities for a wider range
of students along with better job creation in this sector, and subsequently creating more qualified
teachers in this sector.
There was discussion on addressing current problems in the learning environments that are
relevant for female residential students. The public universities in our studies generally are located
outside of Dhaka in remote regions and host female students in residential halls. These female halls
are often located in secluded regions to increase their security. Female students must return to
their residential halls by sunset by institutional policies which restrict access to laboratories. A
participant P30 shared: “Restrictions to access the lab after a certain time led to losing interest.”
Beyond the policy-level restrictions, the students in the residential halls also stated the need for
better internet connectivity. The current challenges in ICT learning were discussed seriously by
several engaged participants. The remote locations of female halls to ensure safety restrict access
to the availability of mobile Internet data from those hostels. P32 shared: “Sometimes the mobile
data doesn’t work properly here.” It also has related disengagement as P14 shared: “There is no proper
network in my hall. In fact, due to this issue, I stopped many online trainings” which may propagate
through their further journeys.
In the design session, P25 stated the importance of “Good internet connection in female halls.” and
participant P14 shared the impact of having limited Internet access, “In my hall, there are utmost
2000 female students. But we have just one internet room. Many of us don’t even know how to operate
computers. It’s because they don’t have the opportunity to learn.” A clear design solution came from
another participant:
“Make a lab for IT students or non-IT students inside the hall or hostel where they can help
us in our lab. Internet speed in the lab is an important issue. In Sylhet, because of the rain the
internet is bad. If we have fiber internet it will be very helpful for us.”—P43, Sylhet.
6.1.3 Facilitation through Mentoring and Role Model. Many participants emphasized the impor-
tance of collaboration through networking and mentorship in our design workshops and suggested
technological solutions for community engagement and addressing underrepresentation of women
in every sector from educational institutions to workplace. A number of participants (16) referred
to collaborative frameworks as a solution approach through the design session. The participants
clearly referred to underrepresentation of women in their letters to M3. They shared concrete
ideas on networking where P43 shared, “Female Teammates Can be a Savior.” P45 and P2 asked for
“support network” and “student forum,” respectively. As a design solution, P48 and P19 referred to
the idea of “website for networking.” It was illustrated with more details:
“An online platform to collaborate between girls in the same department as the student ratio
is low. There can be a website where students can ask questions and female mentors will
reply.”—P32, Sylhet.
Moreover, mentoring support from professionals, role models, and peers was shared as a design
solution by as many as 12 participants. A participant P29 asked for female mentorship to ease up
entrance into the IT industry, P38 asked for mentorship from successful ones while others referred to
mentorship in general. Another participant addresses the requirements clearly as: “I think for solving

these issues, we need some mentors. They can conduct sessions in our university. and give us proper
directions. Also, any event should be published properly so that students can get to know about the
event and can participate.”—P14, Rajshahi. The participants shared information gaps among female
students about ongoing opportunities for the lack of a larger network among women compared to
their male peers.
It shows that the tertiary-level female students are aware of the possible solutions around the
academic challenges through their direct or perceived experiences on existing challenges for WiC.
6.2 Support from Family and Society
6.2.1 Parental Preparedness for Gender-sensitive Upbringing. The gender-sensitive parenting as a
key solution came out among many during the design session while the challenges it created came
out through the letters toward Oporajita and M3. The discussion on parents was not discussed in
previous studies exploring the challenges in the context of Bangladesh [3–7], showing how the FI
allowed participants to talk about challenges that are coming from intimate family members. We
present the challenges followed by the solution approaches participants shared in detail.
The study showed how lack of gender sensitivity limits opportunities for tertiary-level female
students. The limitations vary from parental influence in making decisions about subject choices
(e.g., engineering or not, computer science or not); career choices as female professionals or parental
decision on deciding the time of marriage. A participant shared frankly about subject choices in
her letter to M3: “Some families insist their female children not to study Engineering. They always
say that Engineering is the field for male. Girls will face limitations in the job field if they choose
engineering as a career. Field jobs for women will be full of problems and insecurities. As a result,
females become frustrated and do not want to study engineering.” Apart from subject choices, a
number of participants referred to parents pushing their daughters toward getting married before
graduation. For example, a participant shared how many of her female classmates are not able to
continue their studies as follows:
“As a 9th semester student, I saw a lot of my female friends getting married, they can’t even
