7 Discussion
This work engaged tertiary-level computer science students as the future representatives of the
women in the computing field through FI which has been rigorously illustrated with NLP methods
and relevant visualizations followed by the co-design workshops. The goals of these methods were
to bring out their challenges and solution approaches, respectively.

7.1 Critical Reflection on the Study
Navigating Power Dynamics during Workshops. Following the work of Harrington et al. [106], in
this section, we reflect on the methodology and participant engagement of our study. The diverse
composition of our research team, encompassing various gender, religious, and geographical back-
grounds, has been instrumental in fostering a holistic approach to understanding the experiences of
women in computer science education in Bangladesh. Given our shared yet varied perspectives, we
recognized the need for a methodological design that minimized power dynamics and encouraged
honest reflections. By incorporating indirect inquiry through fictional personas, we facilitated
an environment where participants felt comfortable articulating their experiences and concerns
without fear of judgment or repercussions. Our familiarity with local socio-cultural dynamics
allowed us to identify subtle cues and implicit concerns in participant narratives, adding depth to
the insights gleaned from their letters. Being from the same environment allowed us to create a
supportive and empathetic research setting, which facilitated the participants’ openness in express-
ing their challenges and aspirations within Bangladesh’s unique context. By using FI and indirect
engagement with personas, we minimized direct power imbalances, allowing the participants to
envision solutions free from potential social constraints.
Empowerment through Voice and Imagination. The question arises whether the usage of open
design opportunity provides a blue-sky solution-centric concept, which refers to “thinking not
grounded or in touch with the way things are” [113]. A solution design or thinking of the world
one wishes to operate in may appear as a heavy one where one may not have much power to make
such positive changes, and this thinking can be disempowering from one perspective. Considering
technology as a solution has also been criticized as being a euphemism [114], where in this work,
the thinking takes place around some solution design. However, we have considered the open
page provided in FI as a way to share one’s voice. The participants engagement in this research
reflected their positive engagement in the exploration process. The participants referred to the
flaws in parenting methods and teaching biases in Computer Science and Engineering classes, which
were never reported in prior studies considering WiC in Bangladesh [3–7]. A particular source of
motivation to allow an open thinking space came from the long experience of the first author’s
work on addressing the problem of sexual harassment, where women are the major victims [4, 54,
115]. The social problem of sexual harassment has remained, and in many contexts has worsened,
spreading from physical space to cyberspace, where it spreads rapidly. A solution design approach
to support women to avoid or handle a possible attack may seem useless apparently from outside
since the problem remained. However, when the work was paused, and the researchers were not
sure about the possible impact of this design, the participants approached the researchers and shared
how the discussion gave them strength, hope, and validity [115, 116]. The researchers engaged
in the design process shared how being part of this project made them feel that they were doing
something important. The problem remained, so did the solution design and the discussions around
the design process worked as the activism against a heinous social problem [115, 116]. The social
and structural problems coming from lack of safety, security, and infrastructural support require
large-scale investment and prioritization where policymakers and authorities’ involvement is
needed, a place where there is still a gender imbalance [111]. However, the current limitation should
not be a barrier to dreaming of a better environment where the thought process is liberating, which
is far from the dreams of many others from past generations or who are in different situations. There
are WiC from Bangladesh who are able to enjoy a safe environment pursuing higher education
in foreign regions, as a recent study has shown [112], a dream that has probably stemmed from
seeking change. As researchers, we want to keep the conversations going, even if it feels hard
to achieve, since this discussion is better than silence, which allows problems to persist without

being challenged. Thus, the design process came from opening up a conversation, thinking about a
design solution as an enabler to break the silence that usually remains when it comes to women’s
problems.
Contextualizing the WiC Participants’ Engagement. While prior work [106] found tensions around
the activity structure of participatory design workshops with marginalized communities and
participants indicated that “brainstorming ‘out-of-the-box’ solutions” were not moving toward actual
solutions that can be implemented in near future, our participants did not show any similar behavior.
In contrary, the participants were engaged with the process and many of them wanted to reach
their vision of the world for at some point in various ways suggested for personal, family-level,
social- or policy-level improvements. There could be two possible reasons for this variation. First,
WiC in our study experienced marginalization primarily based on gender, which differs from other
marginalized communities that often face a combination of financial, educational, and gender-based
barriers [13, 14]. Many communities struggling with technology access encounter intersecting
challenges, including economic constraints and limited educational opportunities. In contrast, the
WiC who participated in this study largely did not report financial or educational marginalization.
This may be partly because they have already demonstrated competitive academic success to
gain admission to educational programs, with family support that some other women in similar
age groups might lack, such as those who leave school early due to social pressures like early
marriage [17]. All the public and private universities where we conducted our studies are highly
competitive and prestigious. These women who participated in this study are in a trajectory to enter
the professional field and may contribute to designing changes for future cohorts. Their existing
familiarity and access to technology could explain their interest in envisioning technology enabled
solutions. Second, prior research on Bangladeshi women showed that having a voice to express
what one wants and the ability or freedom to dream of a better world can be considered as an
opportunity in our context. Since many participants were from computer science background, many
of them preferred to ideate technical solutions such as suggesting apps for parents and teachers.
Prior studies engaging the guardians accompanying WiC to attend national-level programming
contests and international robotics competitions show that many parents, especially mothers, were
not allowed to dream, and thus, they wished to make the paths easier for their daughters [3–7, 117].
Many of these parents provided both emotional and financial support. Reflecting on their personal
difficulties was a motivator to work toward thinking of ways that can be useful for their daughters.
In Afghanistan, a similar phenomenon was observed among WiC who were refugees and returnees
themselves and worked to support their junior ones to have easier access to resources prior to the
Taliban Government’s takeover [35]. The work by Kabeer showed how a group of women have
invested in their daughters to ensure that they are well educated and able to earn, ensuring an
enabling environment for their daughters, one that was not present for themselves [118].
Researcher Positionality and Shared Context as Interpretive Tool. Our positionality as researchers
who have navigated similar educational structures equipped us with a unique lens for interpreting
the data. Our reflective approach in this study also acknowledges the dual role of our identities
as both insiders and facilitators. Navigating this space required us to consider how our shared
experiences and social conditioning within the same educational and cultural framework might
subtly shape our interpretations. The balanced dynamics within the research team helped us
remain reflexive throughout the process, allowing us to acknowledge and address any potential
biases that might arise from our shared backgrounds. By actively reflecting on our positionality,
we aimed to strike a balance between empathy and objectivity, ensuring that the participants’
voices were central to our analysis and that our interpretations were grounded in their lived
experiences rather than our own assumptions. Our choice of method reflects a commitment to
respecting the participants’ agency, especially in a setting where critique of authoritative figures

is uncommon. We also recognize the empowering potential of our research activities themselves,
which may have offered participants a rare opportunity to voice and validate their experiences
and solutions. Additionally, as researchers familiar with the lived realities of Bangladeshi WiC, we
were uniquely positioned to interpret and contextualize their design solutions as deeply rooted
responses to structural and cultural challenges they face. This positionality not only enriched our
analysis but also underscored the importance of reflexivity in fostering authentic engagement and
advocating for meaningful technological futures for women in Bangladesh. For example, the ideal
world where a girl can freely walk at night may initially show a complete detachment from the
world of computing, but the researchers could easily vision themselves walking from a late-night
programming class without the worry of getting harassed while riding a public transportation in
Bangladesh. Our shared background allowed us to recognize specific cultural and infrastructural
challenges that might otherwise go unnoticed by external researchers, such as the intricate dynamics
of gender-sensitive teaching and societal expectations surrounding security and mobility for women.
Suggesting a future Bangladesh where teachers and parents are going through psychological tests
may seem initially far-fetched as an idea, but our participants are coming from a generation of
social media usage where continuous activism and community engagement do result in real,
concrete changes. Acid throwing, a violent crime where women’s faces were often disfigured via
throwing acid by perpetrators and 80% of the victims were women, came to a rapid decrease in
the past years in Bangladesh (a drop from 300 to 400 attacks per year to around 30 crimes per
year for the last 6 years), as a direct result of legal changes and awareness generation campaigns
via non-profit and government campaigns [107]. Since the Bangladeshi participants have seen
development from their early years where large-scale social changes are possible when everyone in
society works together, they attempted to use our research study as a platform for advocating their
voices.
Reflexivity in NLP Analysis. Our use of NLP techniques to analyze responses added a structured,
data-driven layer to the qualitative insights, enabling us to capture sentiment variations and compare
thematic patterns across different sites. We also approached this analysis with sensitivity to the
complexities of lived experiences, acknowledging the limitations inherent in sentiment analysis
and the need for nuanced interpretation in such culturally rich and emotionally complex topics. The
data visualizations show us snapshots of participants feelings where they were comfortable sharing
their innermost feelings with a fictional character Oporajita, suggesting perhaps the participants
wants a real-life Oporajita in this generation, just as her fictional ancestor Begum Rokeya proudly
carved the path of feminism in Bangladesh.
Contextual Design for Student Agency. In prior work [110], it has been suggested that “‘poverty
of the mind’ prevents people from embarking on constructive activities” and marginalized com-
munities can choose to “accept and confront their situation and control their own lives by doing
something constructive with whatever few assets they had.” Drawing parallel to this, when we, a
group of students and researchers from South Asia decide to ask our own junior peers about
the challenges they face through FI and utilize their own sentiments as visualizations to draw
the actual feelings of fear or disgust, however, taboo they may be, against their and our own
authority figures it shows a form of agency to utilize all current tools available in the scientific
communities disposal to create policy and technological solutions against the problem of un-
derrepresentation in computing. It also opens the path to collect feedback from ICTD and HCI
community to iterate and improve upon the bare-bone solutions students provided. Although
designing for ideal world for WiC in our co-design workshops might lead to the perception that
the students are asking for a world free from all biases or social prejudices, in reality our students
asked for very simple requirements such as the safety to walk at night on their own and safe
transportation facilities to go to schools. These are their deepest and innermost feelings about the

current circumstances in Bangladesh, which the policymakers have not yet prioritized. However,
we as researchers present their vision as it is in our findings with our ethical obligations. In a
future work, utilizing “think-aloud” strategy [108] where the students would talk about their
solution steps aloud may help to understand their thought process with refined granularity. Also,
the prior work showed that in collectivist societies such as Bangladesh, group studies help to
talk about taboo topics [109], thus we would probably utilize a group setting such as the current
workshops.
7.2 Practical Relevance of the Findings
The in-depth analysis of FI from qualitative methods, illustrated by NLP, shows the myriads
of emotions and sentiments participants shared in their letters. It showed that the sentiments
conveyed in the letters were diverse and emotions such as sadness and anger were present. During
FI, participants wrote letters to fictional characters without fear which helped them to express
their concerns in a safe space. Notably, FI has never been used in WiC context. While prior work
showed the importance of supportive family and teachers [5–7, 17], in our work, we found stronger
emotional responses related to the lack of support from intimate family members and teachers
and advocacy for novel solutions such as counseling and psychological tests for both parents and
teachers. It clearly shows the lack of safe space for women to share the discriminatory behaviors
they have faced in their homes as well as in educational institutes. It requires a broader level of
awareness at family level, institution level, and policy level to ensure gender-sensitive learning
environment. The religious justification of many gendered behaviors has long-term impact on the
learners, and it must be addressed at higher levels. The strong feelings coming from letters of the
young WiC who will enter the job sector soon illustrated by our NLP analysis of sentiments and
emotions show the need to address them urgently. It works as a motivation toward individual,
institutional, and policy-level interventions to address existing challenges.
The co-design method allowed the participants to engage actively to address the problems seeking
their desired changes. The co-design solutions participants asked for reflected a lot about the current
situation and status of WiC in Bangladesh. The set of solutions seeking gender sensitivity among
parents and teachers shows the bruises participants have endured from their previous experiences.
This discussion required courage and shield provided by the FI method considering the close-knit
collectivistic society along with its patriarchal practices [41, 60]; as speaking up against parents and
teachers can be considered taboo in the context of Bangladesh. The designs participants provided
may appear to be simple and direct, but the students honestly raised voices on what they truly want
without any pretense. We acknowledge that the long running societal problems related to WiC are
not easy to address and possibly not through a half-day workshop. However, the workshops are a
starting point and the design contributions and optimism of the young WiC shows how eager they
are to have many of these problems addressed. It also varies from the solutions provided in existing
contextual literature [3, 5, 7, 10, 17, 99]. Existing literature focused mainly on gender-sensitive
policies and awareness generation. While the students in this study also had similar suggestions
they also advocated for major cultural and mindset shifts. They asked for gender neutral parenting in
a cultural context where parents have strong authority over the lives of the children and often make
decisions on behalf of them [102]. A psychological test for parents may appear trivial from outside,
but it is coming from the hope to ensure that the parents are ready to raise their daughters with
strong values. Moreover, they asked for gender-sensitive teaching and continuous evaluation of the
teacher’s values that would not affect their students. Such suggestions coming from participant’s
lived experiences cannot be ignored.
The strongest solutions came from the participants regarding technology to support safe trans-
portation—an ongoing problem that appears to be extremely important to the participants, showing

the continuing insecurities women face in Bangladesh [38, 39]. Transportation and security prob-
lems have been referred to considering attendance of computing-related events and workshops in
different literature in prior work [5, 38, 39]. As our participants are eager to make progress, it is
frustrating to see challenges such as lack of safe transportation remaining as a problem for decades
without any major action taken by the Governing authorities. Moreover, other infrastructural
problems, such as lack of access to labs, difficulty to avail Internet, and so on, have been mentioned
before as a barrier and have not been addressed till now [5, 7, 17]. These problems are comparatively
straightforward to consider if adequate priority and attention are given to them. Thus, there is
a requirement for a gender-sensitive support system for women, enforced at the highest level.
Overall, the solutions, through existing barriers, reflect the current standing of these WiC. The
question remains why these problems are so long standing and what can be done about them.
Currently, the gender-sensitive education policy at the primary and secondary level has shown
great success and progress among female students [59]. It needs to be propagated further with the
help of supportive and required stakeholders. In our study, we have observed that the tertiary-level
students in computing are eager to propose solutions to existing problems. The solutions require
multifaceted approaches from parents, teachers, society members, and adequate authorities. Novel
solutions explored by co-design workshops such as the visual representation of Meena working on
her computer can spark the dream of a future woman in computing. As a solution, gender-sensitive
discussions should continue to ensure the simplest dream of “walking safely back home from work
(read IT Office) on a moonlit night” to come true for any little girl growing up in Bangladesh.
7.3 Relevance of the Research in Current Time
The exploration around the relevance of this work will allow us to understand how this particular
exploration enables the WiC community, stakeholders, policy makers, researchers, which in turn
contributes to the society.
The barriers WiC face have been present from the very early years of computing [100]. Many
of the structural barriers have been addressed while the social barriers have remained [55]. The
number of WiC remained low even in gender-neutral countries like Norway [55, 96]. It shows how
the barriers are deeply rooted and high-level gender-neutrality index is not able to address it. On
the other hand, the number of women were higher in gender-restrictive countries like Saudi Arabia
considering it as a job where women can contribute from home [55]. Here, the higher number of
women in the field contributes to limited mobility aligned by societal barriers. Thus, the gender
neutrality index or the number of WiC does not tell us the entire story.
The societal problems are difficult to address as they are context sensitive in nature. It varies
in regions and evolves over time. In a South Asian country, a woman in computing faces social
barriers that are localized and often is not noticeable by the victims for its long-term existence. A
tertiary-level student in our study, a woman in computing, shared after a discussion with others
that she did not realize that many of the existing practices were barriers. Along with its invisibility,
their barriers evolve over time. In 2024, women are not facing barriers to acquire basic education,
like the battle Begom Rokeya had to fight [66]. The barriers women face today are more subtle. They
are facing subtle disrespect from teachers and peers or having narrower subject choices guided by
parents that appear to be supportive from outside. The key effective way to fight the social barriers
is through generating awareness. The continuing research, discussion, and all forms of engagement
must continue among local and wider communities until majority of the people are conscious of
the existence of prejudices to provide a gender-neutral learning space for WiC.
The HCI, CSCW, and ICTD communities should stand together in ensuring adequate representa-
tion, valuation, and support for WiC anywhere in the world. The problem is not a Bangladeshi or
South Asian problem, it is a global problem and requires a louder voice raised.

8 Lessons Learned and Way Forward
Our study, situated at the intersection of FI, feminist HCI, and NLP, yielded several key lessons about
participant engagement, methodological innovation, and implications for the design of culturally
sensitive NLP tools.
8.1 Applying FI for Participatory Policy Design
In our study, we used FI as a pathway for policy imagining and value articulation. Through letters
addressed to fictional characters like Oporajita (a symbolic feminist figure) and M3 (a patriarchal
persona), students engaged in emotionally rich, speculative storytelling that surfaced deeply
personal reflections about institutional, infrastructural, and societal barriers to their well-being
in computing education. The indirect nature of FI facilitated honest disclosures that participants
may have otherwise withheld, especially in institutional contexts where power imbalances exist.
For example, while challenges like having only one Internet router for thousands of students in
a residential hall may be widely known, they are rarely expressed in formal settings. As insiders
within the institutional context, we were acutely aware of how our presence could influence
participant responses. FI helped mitigate this by shifting the locus of response away from the
researchers and toward imagined futures. For example, students were more comfortable suggesting
psychological evaluations for faculty through fictional letters than they would have been in direct
interviews.
FI thus served as a powerful means of surfacing “unspeakable” or unspoken concerns, and
enabled students to articulate their ideal futures, both for themselves and for the future generations.
Although our focus was the education sector, this methodology has clear potential for domains
such as labor rights (e.g., garment workers), urban planning, and public health, sectors where direct
critique is often inhibited by power relations. Thus, we believe that FI can be further leveraged in
many ways as follows:
—Participatory Policy Design. Especially when working with marginalized communities where
sharing will not be limited through indirections.
—Discussion on Difficult Topics. Exploration on socially or emotionally challenging concepts
where there is a fear of being judged or labeled easily.
—Engagement of Minors. In many cases, the voices of young ones are important, and this method
can open up non-personal sharing through the indirection of FI.
8.2 Insights from Co-design Workshops and Student Reflections
Our co-design workshops, conducted in different regions, affirmed the value of including partici-
pants with varying levels of academic experience. While first-year students often shared optimistic
visions, they also exhibited limited awareness of structural constraints, potentially leading to more
idealistic or far-fetched solutions. However, we adapted our participant recruitment to include
more senior students whose lived experiences brought sharper critique and more grounded rec-
ommendations. This iterative adjustment underscores the importance of sampling diversity when
designing participatory futures. Although many proposed idealistic interventions (e.g., smart bands
for anxiety tracking), they also acknowledged implementation barriers and tradeoffs. Because par-
ticipants were already embedded in the systems they were critiquing, they naturally accounted for
contextual constraints, requiring little external framing from researchers. Their responses reflected
both realism and resilience, contributing to a set of policy and tool design ideas rooted in lived
experience.

8.3 Reflections on NLP Integration and Model Limitations
As we applied NLP tools to analyze students’ letters, we encountered different types of bias:
societal bias reflected in student narratives and model bias evident in model misclassifications,
particularly in culturally specific contexts. These biases represent epistemic concerns, questions
about whose knowledge is valued, and what counts as valid understanding, where models may
systematically fail to recognize or validate the emotional expressions and cultural contexts of
Bangladeshi women students, or succeed, depending on the capability of the models. This highlights
that NLP tools are not neutral technologies but embody particular ways of knowing that may
exclude or misrepresent marginalized communities’ lived experiences. To mitigate these issues, we
approached NLP tools reflexively. First, we conducted a full qualitative analysis before engaging in
any NLP-based modeling. We then compared NLP outputs with human annotations by culturally
embedded researchers. For example, sentiment analysis revealed that participants expressed more
logical, fact-based reasoning when writing to M3, and shared more affective, vulnerable thoughts
with Oporajita. As we engaged with participants from both public and private universities across
different regions, we were reminded of the importance of including diverse perspectives within
our analysis, aligning with our commitment to a collaborative and equitable research process.
These insights emerged not from the models alone, but from our triangulated human–machine
interpretive process.
Furthermore, we identified failure cases and documented specific examples where NLP models
misrepresented or overlooked emotional nuance. Our analysis suggests that open source models,
where pretraining datasets can be scrutinized, are preferable for feminist HCI research in the Global
South. Current auditing tools for pretraining data are insufficiently transparent, limiting critical
analysis of bias propagation. Grounded in that knowledge, we thus call for the development of
culturally sensitive NLP tools, particularly for South Asian languages and social contexts. Building
on work in data feminism and feminist NLP, we advocate for community-led data curation and
model evaluation practices that better represent gendered experiences from underrepresented
regions. We also emphasize several methodological takeaways:
—Unit of Analysis Flexibility. NLP tools should support analysis at varying levels of granularity
(e.g., quote, paragraph, or full document). For example, in our case, quotes were the primary
unit, but aggregating quotes into “letter-level” sentiment scores provided additional insight.
—Transparent Tool Selection. Tool choice was based on availability, pricing, and alignment
with our dataset. This time, we chose open source tools which we could use from Hugging
Face Repository at no-cost which showed high scores on their evaluation set, along with
having the pretraining data publicly available. Future work would benefit from clearer com-
mentary and documentation on tool limitations, particularly when used in marginalized
contexts.
—Pretraining Data Audit. We emphasize the importance of pretraining data auditing tools. While
there are many data and model repositories worldwide, researchers face difficulty to identify
which datasets were used to train which models along with the preprocessing steps.
—Bias-Aware Frameworks. We used a bias-aware framework for examining power relations in
NLP tools to examine our data; however, there was no way to address the power imbalances
even after examining. There is an urgent need for research into tools that not only detect bias
but offer pathways for correction or contextual feedback responses to model developers for
systematic errors.
Our reflections point to the need for a more formalized pipeline for integrating feminist NLP
into participatory feminist HCI research. Such a pipeline should support context-aware annotation,

multilingual processing, and gender bias analysis tools. We complement existing works in these
contexts, by grounding our pipeline in lived, culturally specific narratives and highlighting the
adaptation to South Asian (Bangladesh) context. Ultimately, this reflection reinforces the impor-
tance of researcher positionality and reflexivity in shaping not only the research outcomes but
also the ethical responsibility of advocating for inclusive and contextually relevant technological
solutions.
9 Limitations
This work considers tertiary-level female students only without considering the perspectives of male
peers or other stakeholders around WiC. We wanted to focus entirely on the student perspective
in-depth and hope to consider the other views with same rigor in the future.
10 Conclusion
Grounded in the Bangladeshi context, this study highlights how FI, and co-design can surface
the emotional and structural barriers faced by WiC. Our study offers future female computing
professionals a platform to voice the challenges they have faced and anticipate in their academic
and professional journeys. Their solution ideas, while at an early stage, offer valuable starting
points for future human-centered design and policy efforts. As we invited participants to express
themselves through fictional letters and collaborative design, we were able to uncover perspectives
often overlooked in traditional research. Moreover, with a combination of NLP and qualitative
methods, we captured emotional depth while remaining mindful of the limitations of existing tools.
We hope that our study will be a strong contribution to the careers and lives of Bangladeshi female
computer science students and contribute to broader efforts to amplify WiC voices while adding to
the growing momentum toward making computing education more inclusive and responsive to
the realities of women in the field.

Appendices
A Letters Used in FI
Letters named—Oporajita and M3 used during the Fictional Inquire session. The upper side letter is
from Oporajita representing a supporting persona, and the lower side letter shows the persona of
M3 who uses societal judgements on women’s ability.
Fig. A1. Letters used in Fictional Inquire Session: A Letter from Oporajita.
Fig. A2. Letters used in Fictional Inquire Session: Letter from M3.

B Pictorial Representation of Workshop Steps
FI Steps are represented through hand drawn sketches by researchers conducting the sessions to
clarify the process visually as presented in Table B1.
Table B1. FI Steps with Pictorial Representation
Here the steps of co-design (CD) are presented using a pictorial representation in Table B2 that
includes three major steps.
Table B2. CD Steps with Pictorial Representation
C Emotion Frequency across Location
In the following heatmap of average emotion scores grouped by locations, we can see that neutrality
and sadness are most prominent emotions. Other emotion scores are also fairly consistent over all
locations. To construct the graph, we average the emotion scores over M3 and Oporajita combined
dataset and group by the locations.

Fig. C1. Combined location wise emotion analysis for M3 and Oporajita quotes.
D Emotion Frequency of Challenge Sub-category
When we investigate the emotions associated with each challenge sub-category in M3 vs Oporajita
quotations as presented in Figure D1, we can see that academic challenges came up more in
Oporajita quotes along with disgust and fear-related emotions. The bias category shows disgust
and fear for both Oporajita and M3, but students show anger only to Oporajita. Students talked
about their transportation related fears to Oporajita more too.
Fig. D1. Frequency of challenges sub-category for M3 and Oporajita.
E Average Sentiment per Workshop
The mean sentiment scores across Oporajita, M3, and design workshop shows how neutral, negative,
and positive score values varied across the workshops as presented in Figure E1.

Fig. E1. Sentiment score average, minimum and maximum across various letter response.
F Model Evaluation Guidelines
We followed these guidelines when conducting human annotation in consideration of potential
errors.
(1) Translation changed the meaning of a sentence (slangs were removed, insults toned down,
or emotion softened during automatic translation).
(2) The NLP model misunderstood or erased participant intent (mislabeling a hopeful statement
as neutral, mistranslating gendered expressions, or skipping culturally specific terms).
(3) The model failed to pick up sarcasm or humor (someone said something playful or ironic
and the model interpreted it literally).
(4) The model failed to detect the correct sentiment/emotion (model marking something as
“positive” when it is clearly “negative” or marking something as “neutral” when its frustration
or sadness).
(5) There was disagreement among annotators or the team (if multiple reviewers had different
interpretations of emotion, intent, or meaning). This shows how subjectivity and positionality
affect our work.

quotes.text: Sometimes some developers are very aggressive. If you can’t do something, they will ask “how did you come this far without knowing anything?”
quotes.speaker: S6 · Software professional

quotes.text: I did feel some gender bias even as a Stanford student. In my research lab, I had collaborators and mentors. They had kind of a preconception against me, that I’m a female, I come from a developing country, I must not be very well trained. They were trying to control me, where they would try to modify language. I didn’t feel good about it.
quotes.speaker: Graduate student · ID not specified

quotes.text: I focus on practice. I got better with practice. I keep watching tutorials, reading articles, clearing my concepts, and seeing results, and then I get more feedback and confidence. It has been 2 years, and I’m more confident now. Instead of putting time in tension, it’s much better to go straight to action. I also follow the quote, “Do it anyway.” I used to be afraid that I couldn’t do it, it was taking a lot of time, etc. But now I tell myself to do it anyway. Regardless of how I feel, I just tell myself to do it anyway. I got this growth by practicing more.
quotes.speaker: S8 · Software engineer · Dhaka

quotes.text: We still face a lot of challenges, specially, in engineering, not a lot of girls choose this sector due to our social misleading thoughts. In our society, everybody imagines a successful girl as a doctor, when someone hears that we want to be engineers, people don’t encourage that a lot. Girls are not still free to choose their careers. I have seen a lot of my friends who do not prepare themselves for engineering just for this social issue. As a result, very few girls are seen in our university which is another challenge for this engineering female students.
quotes.speaker: P24 · Student

quotes.text: Speaking for myself, one of the challenges I encountered was getting into an Engineering University. My father wanted me to become a doctor because, according to our society, it was considered more suitable for girls. However, I wanted to explore myself as an engineering student. I had to endure the disapproval of many relatives, and I was afraid of potential embarrassment if I didn’t get accepted. But with sheer determination and a stroke of fate, I made it here, and I’m happy with how things worked out.
quotes.speaker: P50 · Student · Chottogram

quotes.text: We need to encourage other women around us and teach men to restrain gender biases. We need to train more women in the industry so that women can have the opportunity to prove themselves before we move on to normalizing such jobs for both genders.
quotes.speaker: P44 · Student · Chottogram

quotes.text: They think we girls have less analytical skills; we are only capable of remembering things, not implementing or doing something practical. This type of mentality is also noticeable in our respected teachers.
quotes.speaker: P22 · Student

quotes.text: I still have teachers in my classroom who underestimate my ability in lab work. And, on most days, I am tired of being labeled as a “female” engineer, not just an “Engineer”.
quotes.speaker: P44 · Student · Chottogram

quotes.text: Female students are often better at math at the HSC level. But it’s the lab where there seems to be a gap. Developing hands-on skills where the real gap keeps happening. IT education is practical and hands-on, which women lack.
quotes.speaker: S5 · Faculty

quotes.text: In our 1st/2nd semester, we completed some labs based on electrical experiments. We faced unequal opportunities for advancements or leadership roles during those labs. Most of the time, all male students successfully did their experiments with the teacher’s help. However, we, females, failed to do our lab work as a minority group. All male students crowded together during those experiments and completed their experiments as a team. But we are a minority team, and we failed to enter that crowd, hear the teacher’s lecture, and so on.
quotes.speaker: P49 · Student · Chottogram

quotes.text: Still, women have to be back in the residential area very early time, after sunset, though they have work outside.
quotes.speaker: P24 · Student

quotes.text: Although our ACM lab remains open 24 hours for practice sessions and programming-related activities, we (female students) are unable to access the facilities during night time.
quotes.speaker: P36 · Student

quotes.text: Ammu (mother) asked me to apply abroad. She said, why would you waste time staying here? She did not allow any negative comments to reach me.
quotes.speaker: S14 · PhD student

quotes.text: Again, if women get enough support from family and society, they will be able to give enough time and will be able to be serious about their work. In Bangladesh, parents’ ultimate goal is to get married to their daughter to an established person rather than support their daughter in establishing her career. And in the case of marriage, most Bangladeshi men consider looks as a primary standard.
quotes.speaker: P23 · Student · Rajshahi

quotes.text: Current obstacles I’m facing is that career is not the main. They are talking about my age. I kind of agree. I’m not getting younger. I’m likely to get more complications in future. If I do want to extend the family may be its a good idea to start now. But I’m very busy all the time. Right now I’m not mentally prepared for being a parent. They keep telling me that even if I want I will not get a family later.
quotes.speaker: S13 · PhD student · USA

quotes.text: Due to religious attitudes or social norms, many boys do not want to participate properly in class activities with classmates of the opposite sex. In this case, various group activities or discussions are hindered and girls lag behind.
quotes.speaker: P53 · Student · Chottogram

quotes.text: Some teachers behave weirdly with girls. Some religious teachers don’t want to communicate with girls in the class. This is true that for religious purpose, it’s fine. But we went there to study. If teachers don’t want to communicate with us, it will be tough for us to study there.
quotes.speaker: P20 · Student

quotes.text: To address the challenges faced by women, it is important to consider the systemic barriers they encounter. These barriers include unconscious biases, gender stereotypes, limited access to opportunities, and a lack of representation and Mentorship.
quotes.speaker: P28 · Student

quotes.text: Designing Social Media Platform in a way when women achievements in technology are exposed. In terms of perception, Social media plays powerful role. To publish the motivational, spiritual, women success, Cultural influence, and achievements content in social media for parents so that they are motivated for their daughter’s education in science relevant (Strong) subjects to play a vital role in job for future. Not to show the negative content in media eg. Women are vulnerable. As parents are too much influenced by social media, Expose more women to portfolios who are doing computing work all over the world. Its can be done by Building ALGORITHM where women’s positive energy contents should be highlighted.
quotes.speaker: P44 · Student

quotes.text: Also one major issue I face is that, in my daily life I’ve classes from day to afternoon. I love to do problem solving which we say competitive programming here, more specifically we have a separate lab open 24/7 to do practice. But being female, I can’t stay my evening or time during 7pm - 10pm in the lab due to the safety issue I may have to face while returning home. Being female I have to make sacrifices the night time practice at the lab cause I’d face safety issue and the males won’t have to face.
quotes.speaker: P26 · Student · Rajshahi

quotes.text: We have no transportation system right now. I don’t get CNG or rickshaw. I am afraid of bikes but I had to use them because I have no other option. Sometimes you have to make choices to make things work. After working whole day this transportation is a big hassle.
quotes.speaker: S6 · Software professional

quotes.text: My daughter was telling me, when she was walking by the street, a stranger (male) started calling out with “Meow Meaow” sound. She could not ignore it. Later she realized that he made that sound referring to the contact lenses she was wearing. I am so frustrated with society, can’t our daughters walk in peace?
quotes.speaker: P16 · Parent (as published)

quotes.text: Increase surveillance in public transport. Track the transport as the transport will be registered in government application. Application will be featured with transport location. CC camera, emergency button, location tracker in the public buses. After pressing the emergency button it sends the signal to the central through the tracker and sends the notification to the nearest station.
quotes.speaker: P33 · Student

quotes.text: At least from Bangladesh’s perspective, many families want their daughters to become doctors if they are letting their female children pursue higher education. I am not even referring to families who suppress their daughters’ career aspirations, their situation is even more challenging and distressing which is beyond my imagination
quotes.speaker: P30 · Student

quotes.text: Implement awareness programs and training to recognize and challenge unconscious biases in the workplace.
quotes.speaker: P50 · Student

quotes.text: By providing evidence, sharing success stories, and addressing systemic barriers, we can create an environment that promotes gender equality and diversity in the field of computers
quotes.speaker: P49 · Student

quotes.text: Some Male teachers do not provide proper care to the (female) students. I have faced this problem.
quotes.speaker: P47 · Student

quotes.text: Many times girls don’t participate properly in labs or group work because of shyness
quotes.speaker: P53 · Student

quotes.text: The club claims to help sharpen the programming skills of the members, which is why I tried to get into the club for 3 consecutive semesters, but due to my lack of skills, I never even made it through the preliminary levels. I notice a lot of cliques on campus (in my department) that discuss things like coding, competitions, projects, etc, but sadly enough, I don’t ever see any girls in these cliques.
quotes.speaker: P11 · Student

quotes.text: It was great that my husband and I had the same desire to pursue higher education, and luckily, we got admission to the same university.
quotes.speaker: S13 · PhD student

quotes.text: The problem is that family pressure inhibits female students from getting a good education, which results in a lower percentage of women working in computing. Early marriage and dowries are typical barriers that prevent women from participating.
quotes.speaker: P51 · Student

quotes.text: Also not everyone gets the same support and assistance from their family. Sometimes early marriage makes some of them give up on their dream if the in-laws are not that supportive of continuation of studies. Their own family can sometimes oppose the pursuit of their dream
quotes.speaker: P40 · Student

quotes.text: Our superviser was very good to new trainees. If I couldn’t do something the supervisers and the mentors helped with onboarding.
quotes.speaker: S6 · Software professional

quotes.text: In our country there are some safety issues for women. I think this is the main barrier for the women and that’s why family dosen’t want to their child go outside to work.
quotes.speaker: P8 · Student

quotes.text: I never finished the entire programming contest, at the end I stopped participating.
quotes.speaker: S13 · Graduate student

quotes.text: Again, the transportation system in Bangladesh is not suitable for women. Often cases are seen in public transport. In peak time, it is very difficult for women to have ride in bus.
quotes.speaker: P23 · Student

quotes.text: We used to live in Bonosri where boys would make comments about my daughter, now we moved here. The situation is getting worse day by day.
quotes.speaker: S17 · Parent

quotes.text: Any time transportation service. Available seat for females in any transport. Available transport in rural areas. Female Uber or Pathao driver.
quotes.speaker: P37 · Student

quotes.text: First of all, Mr. Mustakim can’t think women are not better than men. He clearly thinks that women just think about their beauty, shopping bla bla bla, I hope, Mr. Mustakim thinks more carefully and respectfully about women. Otherwise, it’s his loss … he should not judge all women with his 3rd class point of views and ideas
